Title: Structured Critical Literature Review Generation via Hierarchical
Contradiction-Aware Synthesis---

Problem
Current automated literature review systems (LLM-based or
retrieval-augmented) produce fluent but shallow summaries — they list findings
paper-by-paper, avoid conflicting results, and fail to organize knowledge into
the canonical sub-topics, debates, and open questions a human reviewer would
surface. No existing system explicitly models contradictions across papers or
generates a structured review with sections like "consensus findings,"
"conflicting evidence," and "methodological gaps."

Hypothesis
A hierarchical, contradiction-aware pipeline that (1) retrieves and
clusters papers by sub-topic, (2) extracts claim-level triples (method, finding,
direction of effect), and (3) explicitly identifies and resolves or flags
contradictions, will produce literature reviews that are rated by domain experts
as more organized, more critical, and more useful than retrieval-augmented
baselines that only summarize per-paper or per-topic.

Method
Stage1 — Hierarchical topic structuring. Given a query (e.g.
"chain-of-thought reasoning"), query a paper corpus (e.g. S2ORC / Semantic
Scholar) and cluster retrieved abstracts using a hierarchical embedding +
LLM-labeling pipeline (HDBSCAN on SBERT embeddings, then GPT-4o-mini assigns
canonical section headings).

Stage2 — Claim extraction and contradiction detection. For each paper, extract
structured claim triples (entity, predicate, direction/sign) via a fine-tuned
DeBERTa-v3 or prompted LLM. Within each sub-topic cluster, compare claim triples
for directional mismatches (e.g. "CoT improves accuracy on GSM8K" vs "CoT does
not improve accuracy on GSM8K"). Flag contradictions with supporting citations
on both sides.

Stage3 — Contradiction-aware synthesis. Generate the review section-by-section
using a controlled generation loop: (a) draft a section from the consensus
claims, (b) conditionally append a "conflicting evidence" sub-section if
contradictions were detected, (c) append an "open questions" sub-section
identifying gaps where evidence is absent or contradictory.

Stage4 — Citation grounding and fact verification. Each generated claim is
back-linked to the original source passage. A lightweight fact-verification step
(NLI-based, e.g. TrueTeacher) verifies whether the generated claim is entailed
by the cited passage. Unverifiable claims are removed or softened.

Dataset / Benchmark- Corpus: Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (S2ORC) — ~8M
papers, with full text when available. Restrict to4-5 well-surveyed domains
(e.g., LLM reasoning, protein folding, adversarial robustness, representation
learning, NLP for low-resource languages).

• Gold-standard reviews: For each domain, collect2-3 human-written survey
papers (e.g. from arXiv, JMLR, ACL anthology). Segment into sections as
ground-truth structure.
• Review quality evaluation set: Construct50 query-review pairs per domain,
each with3 expert ratings along organization, coverage, critical depth, and
usefulness (1–5 Likert).

Evaluation Metrics| Dimension | Metric | How measured |

|---|---|---| | Structure | Section overlap (ROUGE-L / Jaccard on section
headings) | Against human survey TOC | | Coverage | Recall of cited papers from
human survey reference list | Macro-averaged per section | | Critical depth |
Contradiction recall — fraction of known conflicting findings surfaced |
Hand-labeled conflict set | | Faithfulness | % of claims entailed by cited
passages | NLI-based verification + human spot-check | | Overall quality |
Expert rating (1–5) on organization, usefulness | Blind rating by3 domain
experts |

Baselines1. Naive RAG — Retrieve top-20 papers, concatenate abstracts, prompt
GPT-4o to write a review.

2 Per-paper summarization — Summarize each paper individually, then concatenate
under LLM-generated headings (Liu et al.,2024-style).
3 Topic-cluster summarization — Cluster papers by topic, summarize cluster,
then synthesize (similar to Scim,2024).
4 Ours w/o contradiction detection — Same pipeline but skip Stage2
contradiction flagging (ablate the core mechanism).

Ablations- A1: Remove hierarchical clustering → flat topic list (tests whether
hierarchy improves organization).

• A2: Remove fact-verification filter (tests whether filtering reduces
hallucination at the cost of coverage).
• A3: Replace GPT-4o claim extraction with fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 (tests whether
a smaller model suffices).
• A4: Remove contradiction-aware sub-section generation → always write
consensus-only text (tests the value of explicit contradiction flagging vs.
implicit handling).

Expected Failure Modes1. Contradictions are rare or subtle. Most papers in a
well-matured field may agree on fundamentals, leaving little for the
contradiction module to surface. Mitigation: evaluate on at least one rapidly
evolving domain (e.g., LLM reasoning post-2023) where disagreements are common.

2 Claim extraction noise propagates. A false-positive contradiction (two claims
that appear contradictory but differ in experimental setup) degrades the
review. Mitigation: require supporting citations on both sides; add a
confidence threshold for contradiction flagging.
3 Expert raters prefer concise over critical. Human readers may rate a fluent,
uncontroversial summary higher than one that honestly reports messy
disagreements. Mitigation: structure expert evaluation to score critical
depth and usefulness separately from fluency and organization.
4 Structure diversity across human surveys. Two human surveys on the same topic
often use different section taxonomies, making section-overlap metrics noisy.
Mitigation: use macro-averaged ROUGE-L and report variance; also report
expert agreement (Fleiss' κ) on organization.
5 Domain shift. A pipeline tuned on NLP papers may fail for biomedical or
physics literature where citation practices and claim phrasing differ.
Mitigation: hold out one domain for final evaluation only, to measure
generalization.

question: Generate a research proposal on low-resource speech recognition.
answer_a:
Low-Resource Speech Recognition via Decoupled Acoustic-Phonetic Pretraining with
  Targeted Decoder Adaptation## ProblemEnd-to-end automatic speech recognition
 (ASR) for low-resource languages (under10 hours of transcribed speech) suffers
 from a fundamental tension: self-supervised speech encoders (e.g., wav2vec2.0,
    HuBERT) learn rich acoustic representations from unlabeled data, but the
randomly initialized decoder collapses into overfitting on the tiny labeled set
   during fine-tuning. Combined full-model fine-tuning forces the encoder to
 overwrite general-purpose representations to accommodate the decoder's random
  initialization, destroying cross-linguistic transfer. Current methods either
   freeze the encoder entirely (sacrificing language-specific adaptation) or
fine-tune jointly (sacrificing representation generality). The community lacks a
  principled approach that decouples which parameters learn what: the encoder
 should retain its universal acoustic-phonetic knowledge while only the decoder
    and a lightweight adapter should adapt to the target language's phoneme
                             inventory and lexicon.

HypothesisDecoupled training — where a frozen self-supervised encoder feeds a
randomly initialized transformer decoder through a Gated Adapter Module (GAM)
that is the only trained component alongside the decoder — will outperform full
fine-tuning and frozen-encoder baselines on ≤10-hour transcribed benchmarks,
achieving >15% relative word error rate reduction while requiring fewer total
updated parameters. The hypothesis rests on the claim that the encoder's
pretrained representations already contain sufficient phonetic discriminability
for the target language; the bottleneck is the decoder's inability to map those
representations to the target token set without corrupting the encoder.

Method**Stage1: Encoder Selection and Freezing.**Use a multilingual wav2vec2.0
XLSR-53 encoder (pretrained on53 languages, ~600k hours of unlabeled speech).
Freeze all transformer layers. Only the input feature encoder (CNN frontend) and
position embeddings remain trainable to handle language-specific acoustic shifts
(vowel quality, prosody). This is a minimal concession — fewer than2% of total
parameters.

**Stage2: Gated Adapter Module (GAM).**Insert a2-layer bottleneck adapter
between the frozen encoder output and the decoder input, with a learned gating
mechanism:


 z = LayerNorm(encoder_output)
 h = GELU(W_down · z) # bottleneck: d_model →64gate = σ(W_gate · z) # scalar
 per time-stepadapter_output = gate · (W_up · h) + (1 − gate) · z```

 The gate lets the model *per-time-step* decide whether to route through the
 adapter or pass through the original representation unchanged. This prevents
 the adapter from distorting encoder representations on frames where they are
 already well-calibrated for the target language. GAM contributes ~1.2M
 parameters.

 **Stage3: Decoder Training.**The decoder is a6-layer transformer
 (character-level CTC decoder with a language-specific output vocabulary
 of200–400 graphemes). Train the decoder + GAM jointly with CTC loss.

 **Stage4: Optional Self-Training Loop.**After convergence, generate
 pseudo-labels on unlabeled target-language data (if available). Select
 high-confidence frames (posterior >0.9) and retrain GAM + decoder on the
 combined set. This is a *single* iteration — no iterative refinement
 (consistent with the single-run, non-evolving constraint).

 ## Dataset / Benchmark| Dataset | Language | Labeled Hours | Unlabeled Hours |
 Domain |
 |---|---|---|---|---|
 | Common Voice (Swahili) | Swahili |8.2 |120 | Crowdsourced read speech |
 | Common Voice (Tamil) | Tamil |6.8 |85 | Crowdsourced read speech |
 | MLS (Kinyarwanda) | Kinyarwanda |4.5 |0 | Audiobook read speech |
 | FLEURS (Farsi) | Farsi |10.0 |0 | Read speech,5 domains |

 Four languages spanning three language families (Niger-Congo, Dravidian,
 Indo-European) with varied phoneme inventories, ensuring results are not
 language-specific. The split also provides two datasets with unlabeled data
 (for self-training) and two without (for isolated low-resource assessment).

 ## Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Primary / Secondary | Rationale |
 |---|---|---|
 | Word Error Rate (WER) | Primary | Standard ASR metric, directly comparable |
 | Character Error Rate (CER) | Secondary | Captures morphologically rich
 language degradation |
 | Parameter update ratio | Diagnostic | (# updated params) / (# total params),
 to verify decoupling claim |
 | Time-to-convergence | Diagnostic | Training steps to reach best WER,
 measuring optimization stability |

 All WER/CER reported with95% confidence intervals from3 random seeds per
 condition. Statistical significance assessed with paired bootstrap resampling
 (p <0.05).

 ## Baselines1. **Full Fine-Tuning (FFT).** Unfrozen XLSR-53 encoder + random
 decoder. Standard approach for low-resource ASR.
 2. **Frozen Encoder (FE).** Entire encoder frozen, train decoder only.
 Represents the current state-of-the-art for extremely low-resource settings.
 3. **Adapter without Gate.** GAM without the per-time-step gating mechanism
 (constant residual). Isolates the contribution of the gating mechanism.
 4. **Full Adapter (no bottleneck).** Adapter with d_model → d_model (no
 bottleneck). Tests whether the bottleneck is necessary or if a full-rank
 adapter achieves the same result with more parameters.

 ## Ablations| Ablation | What changes | What it tests |
 |---|---|---|
 | **No GAM** | Remove adapter entirely; train decoder directly on frozen
 encoder output | Whether any adapter is necessary at all |
 | **No gate** | Remove gating; use standard residual adapter | Contribution of
 per-step gating |
 | **Bottleneck width** | Vary bottleneck dim:16,64,256 | Sensitivity to
 compression; the64-dim choice |
 | **Trainable CNN frontend off** | Freeze the input feature encoder entirely |
 Whether the2% parameter allowance matters |
 | **No self-training** | Skip pseudo-label Stage4 | Contribution of the
 single-round self-training |

 ## Expected Failure Modes1. **Language mismatch in the pretraining corpus.**
 XLSR-53 covers53 languages. If the target language is typologically distant
 from all covered languages (e.g., a tonal language with no tonal-language
 pretraining data), the frozen encoder may lack the relevant phonetic
 discriminability. Expect WER degradation on such languages; the GAM cannot
 invent acoustic distinctions the encoder never learned. Mitigation: select
 languages with varying distance from XLSR-53 coverage; report WER vs.
 phylogenetic distance as a diagnostic.

 2. **GAM gate collapse.** The gating mechanism may converge to a trivial
 solution: gate ≈0 everywhere (bypass adapter entirely, equivalent to frozen
 encoder baseline) or gate ≈1 everywhere (disabling the residual connection,
 making GAM a standard adapter). Monitor gate statistics over training; if
 all-time-step mean gate lies outside [0.2,0.8], training is degenerate.

 3. **Self-training confirmation bias.** The single self-training iteration may
 reinforce decoder errors if the pseudo-label threshold (0.9) is too permissive
 or too strict. Character-level analysis of pseudo-labeled vs. ground-truth
 distribution on a held-out subset will quantify error amplification.

 4. **Catastrophic forgetting through CNN frontend.** Although only the CNN
 frontend is trainable (2% of parameters), aggressive learning rates could
 still shift the feature distribution enough to degrade downstream
 representations. Monitor encoder output norm drift as a diagnostic.

 ## Limitations- The method assumes access to a pretrained multilingual speech
 encoder. Languages with no phylogenetic overlap to any pretraining language
 remain out of scope. The method does not propose new pretraining; it exploits
 existing frozen representations.
 - Character-level CTC decoding imposes a conditional independence assumption
 that degrades on languages with long-range phonological dependencies (e.g.,
 vowel harmony in agglutinative languages). A future iteration would replace
 CTC with a transducer or attention-based decoder, but that would conflate
 representation adaptation with decoding architecture changes.
 - The single-round self-training (Stage4) is deliberately limited to remain
 consistent with the non-evolving design constraint. Multi-round self-training
 or iterative pseudo-label refinement could yield additional gains but is
 excluded by experimental design.
 - Evaluation is limited to read-speech domains (Common Voice, MLS, FLEURS).
 Conversational and noisy-condition generalization is not tested. Performance
 on spontaneous, code-switched, or child speech is unknown.
 - The adapter adds ~1.2M parameters and one forward pass per frame (two linear
 layers + gating). Real-time factor impact is not measured; latency-critical
 deployments would need a separate efficiency analysis.

Research Proposal: Confidence-Gated Iterative Pseudo-Labeling with
Phoneme-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource ASRTitle: Semi-Supervised
Self-Training with Audited Pseudo-Labels and Phoneme-Preserving Augmentation for
Under-10-Hour Speech Recognition---

Problem
State-of-the-art ASR systems (e.g., Whisper, wav2vec2.0) degrade
catastrophically when fine-tuned on fewer than10 hours of transcribed speech.
Two failure modes dominate: (1) overfitting to the small labeled set, and (2)
confirmation bias in self-training, where the model reinforces its own errors
through noisy pseudo-labels on unlabeled data. No existing method jointly
addresses label quality and data diversity in the under-10-hour regime on a
single pipeline.

Hypothesis
A self-training loop that audits pseudo-labels through a separate
confidence calibrator (rather than the ASR model's own softmax) and couples them
with phoneme-preserving augmentations (time-stretch, pitch-shift, and speed
perturbation clipped to per-phoneme duration bounds) will outperform standard
pseudo-labeling and unsupervised pre-training when labeled data ≤10 hours. The
key claim: auditing prevents confirmation bias, and phoneme-constrained
augmentation prevents the augmentations from destroying linguistic content that
the small labeled set cannot recover.

Method1. Seed model — Fine-tune a small SSL encoder (wav2vec2.0 Base, ~95M
params) on the labeled set (≤10 h). Use a single linear projection head.

2 Pseudo-labeling loop (3 rounds):

• Decode the unlabeled pool with the current model (CTC greedy decoding).
• Audit each pseudo-label: pass the logits to a separate lightweight confidence
estimator (a2-layer MLP over mean-pooled encoder features, trained on the
seed set's held-out fold) and retain only utterances where estimated
confidence ≥0.9 threshold.
• Combine audited pseudo-labeled utterances with the original labeled set.

3 Phoneme-constrained augmentation — Before each training epoch, apply:

• Time stretching (0.85x–1.15x) with per-phoneme duration floor.
• Pitch shift (±2 semitones).
• Speed perturbation (0.9x–1.1x).
• Constraint: a forced-alignment phoneme recognizer (pretrained multilingual)
verifies that the augmented audio's phoneme sequence matches the original;
discard any augmentation where >20% of phonemes shift.

4 Re-train the SSL encoder + projection head from the seed checkpoint on the
combined (labeled + audited pseudo-labeled + augmented) data. Repeat for3
rounds.

Dataset / Benchmark- Primary: Common Voice (Tamil, Sinhala, Catalan, Kyrgyz —4
languages with2–8 h of validated train data each). Evaluate on each language's
official dev/test splits.

• Secondary (sanity check): FLEURS10-hour subset for2 additional languages
(Swahili, Bengali).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Purpose |

|---|---| | Character Error Rate (CER) | Primary metric; report mean ± std over3
seeds. | | Word Error Rate (WER) | Secondary, for languages with space-delimited
orthography. | | Pseudo-label acceptance rate | Diagnostic: % unlabeled
utterances retained per round. | | Oracle accuracy of accepted pseudo-labels |
Diagnostic: if a held-out reference exists for the unlabeled pool, measure what
fraction of accepted labels are correct. |

Report effect sizes with95% bootstrap confidence intervals across seeds.

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|---|---| | Seed-only (fine-tune on labeled data only, no self-training) | Lower
bound — isolates the value of unlabeled data. | | Standard pseudo-labeling (no
auditing, no augmentation) | Ablates the audit mechanism. | | No-augmentation
self-training (audit + pseudo-label, no phoneme constraint) | Ablates the
augmentation contribution. | | SpecAugment self-training (SpecAugment instead of
phoneme-constrained augmentation) | Compares against a widely-used augmentation
baseline. | | wav2vec2.0 Base fine-tuned on full Common Voice (where available,
e.g., Catalan ~80 h) | Upper bound — what performance looks like with abundant
data. | | Whisper Small zero-shot | Compares against a strong multitask model
that has never seen the target language during adaptation. |

Ablations1. Audit threshold sweep — Vary the confidence threshold
(0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95) on one language to measure the precision-recall trade-off in
pseudo-label acceptance.

2 Augmentation constraint strength — Compare the phoneme-preserving constraint
against an unconstrained version (same augmentations, no phoneme-validity
check).
3 Number of self-training rounds — Compare1,2,3, and5 rounds on one language to
measure when performance plateaus or degrades.
4 Size of labeled seed — Sub-sample to1 h,2 h,5 h on a language with8 h
available, and measure whether the method's advantage grows as labeled data
shrinks.

Expected Failure Modes1. Phoneme-constraint too aggressive — The multilingual
forced-aligner may have poor accuracy on a target language it was not trained
on, causing most augmentations to be discarded. Mitigation: Relax the threshold
to40% phoneme shift tolerance; also measure the discard rate and report it.

2 Confidence estimator is poorly calibrated — On languages far from the seed
set, the auditor may either accept noisy labels (false positive) or reject
correct ones (false negative). Mitigation: Use temperature scaling (Platt

long-range reasoning) saturate earlier than others (e.g., syntactic fluency,

precise structural causes of saturation in small models and design targeted
interventions that reallocate limited capacity to the binding constraints?

Primary hypothesis: The performance ceiling in small models is driven
by capacity-competition between world-knowledge memorization and compositional
reasoning pathways, not by a global lack of parameters. When a small model
saturates, additional training data primarily overfits its already-congested
feedforward memory (FFN layers) while the attention-based compositional routing
remains underutilized.

functions — compressing factual knowledge into a fixed, non-parametric memory
(retrieval augmentation with a small bottleneck) and freeing FFN parameters for
compositional reasoning — will raise the ceiling by10–20% on reasoning-heavy
benchmarks while matching or exceeding baselines on factual recall.

long-range reasoning (5+ hops), and in-context learning. Use influence functions
and representation similarity (CKA between hidden states at different data
scales) to identify which layers/modules saturate first and correlate with which

factual recall while lower attention layers saturate for compositional
reasoning.

Research Proposal: Compositional Grounding for Multi-Step Reasoning in
  Tool-Augmented Language Agents## ProblemLarge language models (LLMs) achieve
  strong performance on isolated reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH) but
  degrade sharply when deployed as agents that must interleave reasoning with
     external tool calls. The core challenge is not reasoning capacity but
 compositional grounding: the agent must decide when to rely on a tool, how to
 format its output for the tool, and how to integrate the tool's response back
  into its reasoning trace — all while maintaining coherence across a growing
    action history. Current agent frameworks handle this with brittle prompt
  engineering (ReAct, Reflexion) that breaks under distribution shift, and no
  existing benchmark jointly measures the reasoning–tool–memory triplet under
                      controlled compositional variations.

HypothesisAgents fail on multi-step reasoning-with-tools not because the
underlying LLM lacks reasoning ability, but because the compositional interface
between reasoning and tool-use is undertrained. Specifically, we hypothesize
that a compositional-granularity taxonomy — decomposing tasks by (a) number of
tool-call decision points, (b) depth of tool-output integration (surface-passing
vs. structural reformatting), and (c) recency-dependency of prior tool outputs —
predicts agent failure modes better than aggregate accuracy, and that a
structured training curriculum built on this taxonomy can close the gap without
architectural changes.

MethodWe propose a three-phase methodology:

Phase1 — Taxonomy and Benchmark Construction. Define a3 ×3 ×3 design space:


 Dimension               Levels
 Decision points (D)     1,3,5 tool-call junctures
 Integration depth (I)   Surface (pass tool output verbatim into next prompt),
                         Reformatted (extract key fields and restructure),
                         Aggregated (merge multiple tool outputs before
                         reasoning)
 Recency dependency (R)  Independent (each step depends only on initial state),
                         Chain-1 (depends on immediately prior tool output),
                         Chain-3 (depends on outputs from three steps back)


From this space we sample9 task families (one per D-I-R cell) covering
calculator, retrieval, code-execution, and database-query tools, creating1800
instances (200 per cell,20 held-out per cell for validation).

Phase2 — Failure-Mode Profiling. Run a representative set of current agent
frameworks (ReAct, Reflexion, Plan-and-Solve, Tree-of-Thought with tool calls)
across all1800 instances using GPT-4o and Llama-3-70B. Record per-instance:
final accuracy, step-wise tool-call accuracy, and integration fidelity (whether
the agent correctly used the tool output in the subsequent reasoning step). Map
failures onto the D-I-R cell structure.

Phase3 — Targeted Curriculum Training. Construct a training curriculum ordered
by the failure-rate gradient from Phase2 (easiest cell first). Fine-tune a base
Llama-3-8B on this curriculum with a loss that reweights steps where integration
fidelity is low. Evaluate held-out instances from each cell and compare to
uniform-data fine-tuning and prompt-based baselines.

Dataset / BenchmarkNo existing benchmark covers the D-I-R compositional design
space. We build CompoTool-1800:

 • Tool types: calculator (Python eval-like), knowledge retrieval (Wikipedia
   snippet API), code execution (sandboxed Python exec), database query (SQLite
   over synthetic tables)
 • Task templates: multi-hop arithmetic with calculator calls, fact-verification
   with retrieval + calculator, data-analysis pipelines with SQL + Python,
   mixed-tool planning tasks- Splits:1600 train (sampled uniformly across
   cells),200 validation (20 per cell held out for controlled evaluation)
 • Contamination check: all tool outputs are procedurally generated; no overlap
   with public datasets## Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: Cell-level accuracy
   (average per D-I-R cell) — the main metric that tests whether the taxonomy
   captures failure patterns2. Integration fidelity (per-step): binary indicator
   of whether the agent correctly incorporated tool output into the next
   reasoning step, measured by an automated verifier3. Tool-call precision:
   fraction of tool calls that used the correct tool with the correct
   arguments4. Composite difficulty score: weighted average across D, I, R
   dimensions, used to test monotonicity (accuracy should decrease as composite
   score increases)

 5 Cross-model rank consistency: Spearman correlation between model rankings on
   CompoTool-1800 vs. existing agent benchmarks (AgentBench, ToolBench) to
   validate that our benchmark measures something not already captured##
   Baselines1. ReAct (Yao et al.,2023) — thought–action–observation loop,
   zero-shot2. Reflexion (Shinn et al.,2023) — verbal self-reflection on
   failures3. Plan-and-Solve (Wang et al.,2023) — plan-first then execute4.
   Tree-of-Thought with tool-call leaves (Yao et al.,2024 variant) —
   breadth-first search over reasoning + tool paths5. Direct prompting (no agent
   scaffolding) — single-prompt with interleaved instructions, included to
   measure the ceiling of in-context abilityAll baselines run with GPT-4o and
   Llama-3-70B. The Phase3 fine-tuned model is compared against a uniform-data
   fine-tuned Llama-3-8B (same compute budget) and the base Llama-3-8B with
   ReAct.

Ablations1. No tool-output integration verifier: remove the step-wise fidelity
weighting from the curriculum loss to isolate its contribution2. Random-order
curriculum: shuffle the cell ordering in Phase3 to test whether the
difficulty-gradient ordering is necessary3. Single tool type: restrict training
to only calculator tasks to measure cross-tool generalization4. No fine-tuning:
compare the fine-tuned model to the base model with a hand-crafted prompt
template for each cell (rule-based adaptation of ReAct)

Expected Failure Modes1. Surface integration ceiling: agents that pass tool
outputs verbatim without structural reformatting may hit an accuracy ceiling
around D=3, I=Reformatted — the taxonomy predicts this, and it may be
irreducible with current transformer architectures2. Recency decay: Chain-3
instances will likely show accuracy near random beyond4–5 steps regardless of
model size, consistent with known attention sink and lost-in-the-middle
effects3. Curriculum overfitting: the fine-tuned model may specialize to the
D-I-R cell boundaries and fail on instances that fall between cells (e.g., D=2,
I=Reformatted, R=Chain-2 — an untrained cell)

 4 Verifier noise: the automated integration-fidelity verifier may itself err on
   complex cases (e.g., when a tool output is correct but the agent uses it
   indirectly), introducing label noise into the curriculum loss## Limitations1.
   Tool repertoire is fixed: only four tool types, all with clean input/output
   schemas. Real-world agents interact with dozens of heterogeneous, poorly
   documented APIs. Generalization to open-ended tool sets is untested.
 5 Synthetic instance generation: procedurally generated tasks lack the
   ambiguity of human-generated queries. Performance on CompoTool-1800 may
   overestimate real-world robustness.
 6 No multi-turn user interaction: the benchmark assumes a single user query
   with a linear tool-use trace. Conversational agents that revisit earlier
   steps or take user feedback mid-trajectory are out of scope.
 7 Single-turn fine-tuning: the curriculum training uses offline supervised
   learning on successful trajectories. Online (RL-based) methods such as
   outcome-driven reward modeling may yield different conclusions about the
   taxonomy's utility.

   to70B+ models, which exhibit different error patterns (more false positives
   than false negatives in tool-call decisions). The baseline profiling with
   GPT-4o and Llama-3-70B partially addresses this, but the fine-tuning
   experiment is limited to8B.

Title**"Plan-Trace-Verify: A Controlled Study of Multi-Step Compositional
Reasoning in LLM Agents Under Distractor Conditions"**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based agents today are deployed on tasks that require chaining
multiple reasoning steps (e.g., "book a flight, check the weather at the
destination, then find restaurants within budget"). These agents frequently fail
not because individual steps are hard, but because they lose the thread when
intermediate results contradict expectations or when irrelevant context
(distractors) is injected mid-trajectory.

The core problem: existing benchmarks evaluate reasoning in clean, single-turn
settings (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, HotpotQA), but agentic reasoning involves iterative
plan-trace cycles where earlier outputs become inputs to later steps. We lack a
controlled benchmark that isolates the effect of "distractor injection" —
irrelevant or misleading intermediate observations — on compositional reasoning
accuracy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
H₁ (Primary): Injecting task-irrelevant but semantically plausible
observations mid-trajectory degrades LLM agent compositional reasoning accuracy
by ≥25% relative to the no-distractor baseline, even when the underlying
reasoning path is unchanged.

H₂ (Mechanism): The degradation is primarily driven by retrieval interference
(the agent attends to distractor tokens in subsequent reasoning steps) rather
than plan corruption (the agent incorrectly revises its plan). This implies that
improving selective attention (e.g., structured memory) will help more than
improving planning ability.

H₃ (Mitigation): A simple Plan-Trace-Verify loop — where the agent explicitly
writes down its plan before execution, traces each step against the plan after
receiving observations, and verifies consistency before proceeding — recovers
≥80% of the performance gap relative to the no-distractor baseline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Framework: Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV)

We define three agent strategies to compare:

1 Direct-ReAct (baseline): Standard ReAct-style agent — thinks, acts, observes
in a flat loop with no explicit plan tracking.
2 Plan-then-Execute (ablation control): The agent writes a plan (as pseudocode

re-check consistency after each observation.
3 Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV) (proposed): The agent:

postconditions for each step.

and SQL grammar tokens, combined with a lightweight prefix that encodes
question–column alignment scores, will eliminate schema hallucination and
improve logical correctness on compositional queries. The schema constraint is a
hard filter — the decoder can only emit tokens that appear in the active
database schema or the SQL keyword vocabulary — so hallucination is structurally
impossible. The prefix module learns a soft alignment between question spans and
table/column candidates, providing the decoder with grounded attention without
requiring a separate entity-linking pass.

schema (S = {T_1, \dots, T_k}) where each table (T_i) has columns ({c_{i1},
\dots, c_{im}}), we compute a question-aware schema representation. Each column
(c_{ij}) is encoded as a concatenation of its name, type, and a sampled cell
value. A bi-affine scorer computes alignment scores between each question token
and each column, producing a schema-grounded prefix vector that is prepended to
the decoder's hidden states at every decoding step.

vocabulary is masked to the union of:

 • SQL reserved keywords (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, etc.)
 • Table names in (S)
 • Column names in (S)

   log-probability. This mask is recomputed per example since each database has
   a different schema.

alignment loss that minimizes the KL divergence between the bi-affine attention
weights and a soft alignment derived from the gold SQL's column references. The
two losses are summed with equal weight.

also evaluate on Spider-Syn (synonym-substituted questions) and Spider-DK
(domain-knowledge questions) to test robustness to lexical variation and
implicit reasoning. For cross-domain generalization, we report on the Spider-CG
split (cross-domain compositional generalization). Execution accuracy on the dev
set is the primary metric.

execution output matches the gold output on a held-out SQLite instance. The
primary metric.

   standard T5 decoder; rejects invalid SQL prefixes. Direct comparison for

condition. The mask is also schema-specific and must be recomputed per database,
adding a pre-processing step at inference. The bi-affine prefix network is
trained on gold alignments derived from the SQL, which are noisy: multiple
column references in a long query may align to overlapping question spans.

views or nested subqueries with aliases in a schema-not-present way; these

   productions instantiate the motifs from stage1. Grammar weights are set
   proportional to motif frequencies observed in the repository corpus, so
   skeletons mirror real code structure.
 3 Constrained abstract-execution trace. For each generated skeleton, an
   abstract interpreter computes a symbolic state (variable ranges, type
   constraints, path feasibility) before any concrete values are chosen. Invalid
   skeletons (unreachable branches, type mismatches) are pruned. Remaining
   skeletons are concretized with random concrete values drawn uniformly from
   the state constraints.
 4 IO-pair generation. Execute each concretized program on5–20 random inputs
   (also drawn from the constraint-satisfying distribution) to obtain
   input–output pairs. Programs that crash, loop beyond a step limit, or produce
   non-deterministic results are discarded.
 5 Fine-tuning. Take a base code LLM (e.g., CodeLlama-7B or DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B)
   and fine-tune on the (program, input–output specification) pairs. The
   specification is formatted as a docstring with Args: / Returns: sections plus
   one-shot examples, mirroring the HumanEval prompt style.

Dataset / Benchmark

 • **Synthetic corpus:**200 K program–IO pairs produced by the pipeline
   above.100 K from high-frequency motifs,100 K from long-tail motifs (frequency
   <1% in the corpus) to stress generalization.
 • Evaluation benchmarks: HumanEval+ (167 problems, stricter test harness),
   MBPP+ (399 problems, sanitized tests), and a custom Motif-Probe suite of80
   small programs each targeting exactly one motif from the catalogue.
 • Naturalness check: Perplexity on held-out GitHub Python files (the Stack v2
   filtered subset) to measure distributional alignment.

Evaluation Metrics

 • Pass@1 on HumanEval+ and MBPP+ (n=20 samples, temperature0.2).
 • Per-motif accuracy on Motif-Probe (macro-F1 across the80 probes).
 • Program naturalness — cross-entropy difference between the fine-tuned model
   and the base model on the held-out corpus (lower is more natural).
 • Data efficiency — performance after50K,100K,200K synthetic samples vs.
   equivalent-size subsets of web-scraped data.

Baselines

 1 Base model (no fine-tuning) — establishes a floor.
 2 Web-scraped fine-tuning — same model, same compute budget, trained on
   randomly sampled code from The Stack v2 (matched to200K tokens).
 3 Docstring-harvested data — programs with natural-language docstrings from
   GitHub, stripped to (docstring, body) pairs.
 4 Random grammar baseline — programs generated from an unweighted CFG without
   the abstract-execution guard (no constraint pruning, no motif-frequency
   weighting).

Ablations (within the proposed method)

 • W/o concrete execution guard — skip the abstract-interpretation prune step;
   include all syntactically valid skeletons even if they are infeasible.
 • W/o motif weighting — uniform grammar weights instead of
   frequency-proportional weights.
 • W/o long-tail oversampling — generate only from high-frequency motifs.

Expected Failure Modes

 • Abstract interpreter may be too conservative, pruning programs that are valid
   but whose symbolic state is imprecise, narrowing coverage.
 • Motif catalogue may overfit the static-analysis pass; motifs that appear
   frequently in source code may be trivial for the model already, yielding no
   learning signal.
 • Concretized IO pairs for long-tail motifs may be too sparse or too similar to
   each other, providing weak supervision.
 • The model may learn to exploit spurious correlations in the synthetic prompt
   format (e.g., fixed Args: / Returns: layout) and fail on the varied style of
   HumanEval+ docstrings.

Limitations

 • The pipeline requires a static-analysis infrastructure (AST visitor +
   abstract interpreter) that must be re-targeted per language; this proposal
   covers only Python.
 • Motif frequencies are derived from public GitHub repositories, which may not
   reflect internal or domain-specific codebases (e.g., scientific computing,
   embedded systems).
 • Execution guard assumes determinism; programs that rely on randomness or
   external state (I/O, wall-clock time) are discarded, biasing the corpus
   toward pure functions.
 • The approach does not model program correctness beyond IO matching — programs
   that pass the IO tests for the provided inputs may still contain subtle bugs
   not exposed by the generated inputs.
 • Data-efficiency comparisons are confounded by token count: synthetic programs
   are typically shorter than human-written files, so200K synthetic samples
   represent fewer total tokens than200K web-scraped files.
 • No evolution memory applied; this is a single-pass proposal that does not
   learn from past failures or refine its motif catalogue across runs.

Research Proposal: Synthesizing Failure-to-Repair Trajectories for Improving
Code LLM Reasoning## Title
Trajectory-for-Code: Self-Supervised Synthesis of
Debugging Trajectories for Robust Code Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLMs are predominantly trained on (instruction,
correct_solution) pairs, either from human sources (e.g., StarCoder data) or
synthetic pipelines (e.g., CodeAlpaca, OSS-Instruct). This outcome-only
supervision has two limitations:

1 Brittle reasoning on hard problems — When the model's first attempt is wrong,
it has no training signal for how to recover. It was never shown buggy
attempts, test failures, or the iterative debugging steps that lead to
correct code.
2 Overconfident generations — Models trained exclusively on correct outputs
lack calibrated uncertainty about when their code is likely wrong, and cannot
self-correct without an external oracle.

Gap: While self-debugging and self-refine methods exist at inference time, no
systematic study has asked whether training on synthesized debugging
trajectories (attempt → test failure → bug analysis → repair → verified fix)
improves a model's code reasoning and self-correction ability at both train and
test time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary: Fine-tuning a code LLM on self-synthesized debugging
trajectories — sequences where the model sees its own buggy attempt, test
failure signal, natural-language bug explanation, and a corrected solution —
improves pass@1 on held-out reasoning benchmarks by ≥5% over fine-tuning on the
same volume of (instruction, correct_code) synthetic data alone.

Secondary: The same training yields a measurable improvement in self-correction
(ability to improve a generation given test feedback at inference time) without
requiring an external verifier during training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Trajectory Synthesis Pipeline (fully automated, no human
labels)

Given a base code LLM (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct or CodeLlama-7B) and a
set of programming problems from a training split (e.g., APPS training set or a
subset of CodeContests):

1 Attempt: Sample $k=5$ solutions per problem from the model (temperature0.8).
2 Execute: Run each solution against the problem's test cases. Categorize as
pass or fail. Collect the failing test input, expected output, and actual
output.
3 Bug analysis prompt: For each failing solution, prompt the model: "Explain
why this code fails on the given test. Identify the specific bug." This
produces a natural-language bug description. Filter by a lightweight check —
the description must mention the relevant variable or line (heuristic).
4 Repair prompt: Prompt the model: "Given the buggy code, the test failure
details, and the bug explanation above, write a corrected version." Execute
the corrected version; keep only repairs that pass all tests.
5 Assemble trajectory: (problem → buggy_code → test_failure → bug_analysis →
corrected_code). Also include the successful (problem → correct_code) paths
as positive examples.

Yield: ~3–5× more training sequences per problem (one correct path + several
repair trajectories).

To control quality, discard trajectories where:

• The bug analysis is empty or generic (<10 tokens).
• The repair still fails any test case.
• The buggy code has a syntax error (trivial).

Stage2 — TrainingFine-tune the base model on a mixture:

-50% standard (instruction, correct_code) pairs from the same problem set-50%
trajectory data (each trajectory formatted as a multi-turn chat: user → problem,
assistant → code, user → test fails with details, assistant → bug analysis, user
→ fix it, assistant → corrected code)

Train for2 epochs. Use a replay buffer where trajectory data is sampled
proportional to the number of repair steps (more steps → higher weight). Compare
against a control fine-tuned on the same total tokens but only (instruction,
correct_code) pairs.

Stage3 — EvaluationEvaluate on held-out benchmarks (see below). Measure both
static pass@k and self-correction pass@1: allow the model one additional attempt
with test failure feedback.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Training data source:

• CodeContests (training split) ~13K problems with test cases — diverse
difficulty, multiple languages.
• Supplement with APPS (training split) ~5K problems for coverage.

Evaluation benchmarks (held-out, no test set overlap):

• HumanEval+ —164 problems with80× more test cases (EvalPlus). Measures
functional correctness.
• MBPP+ —399 problems with enriched tests.
• LiveCodeBench — recent competitive programming problems, tests recency and
generalization.
• CodeContests (test split) —165 problems.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Description |

|---|---| | pass@1 | Standard functional correctness on first sample
(temperature0.2, greedy) | | pass@5 | Any of5 samples passes (temperature0.8) |
| self-correct pass@1 | First sample + one repair round given test failure
feedback. Measures the model's ability to debug its own output. | | trajectory
efficiency | % of synthesized trajectories that produce valid repairs after one
pass (measures pipeline quality) | | calibration error | Expected Calibration
Error (ECE) on the model's confidence vs. pass rate, to test whether training on
failures produces better-calibrated models |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Base model (no fine-tuning) — e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct2.
Standard SFT — fine-tuned on (instruction, correct_code) only, matching total
tokens3. Code Alpaca / OSS-Instruct style — synthetic instruction–code pairs
from a teacher model4. Self-play w/o trajectories — generate correct code,
filter by tests, train on that (no failure data)

5 CodeRL baseline — actor-critic with test pass/fail as reward (uses RL, not
SFT on trajectories)
6 Self-Debugging (inference-only, no trajectory training) — to isolate training
benefit---

Ablations1. Remove bug-analysis step: train on (problem → buggy → repair)
without the natural-language bug explanation. Isolates the value of intermediate
reasoning.

2 Remove failure signal: train on (problem → repair) only — show the model the
correct code without showing the failure context.
3 Trajectory ratio sweep: vary the % of trajectory data in the mix
(10%,30%,50%,70%) to measure diminishing returns.
4 Model scale: replicate on1B,7B, and14B models to test whether trajectory
training helps more at smaller scales (where self-correction is hardest).
5 Oracle repair vs. model repair: replace the model's own repair step with
GPT-4's repair to measure the ceiling (is the bottleneck synthesis quality or
training itself?).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Repair data is too easy — the model generates obviously buggy code
that it easily fixes, so trajectories are trivial. | Filter trajectories by the
edit distance of the repair; keep only those with non-trivial changes (>3 tokens
different). | | Model learns to generate buggy code to get repair signal —
exploits the training setup. | Keep the50% standard SFT mix as a regularizer;
never reward buggy-only generations. | | Synthetic bug analysis is hallucinated
— the explanation sounds plausible but is wrong. | The repair step must produce
executed correct code; wrong explanations that still lead to correct repairs are
harmless, and wrong explanations that mislead the repair will be discarded. | |
No improvement on single-turn pass@1 — the benefit only shows in multi-turn
self-correction. | Acceptable if self-correction improves, but the hypothesis
requires ≥5% improvement on pass@1. If self-correction improves without pass@1,
refine the hypothesis. | | Small model can't produce valid bug explanations (<1B
parameters) leads to low-quality trajectories. | Restrict the study to ≥7B
models; use1B as an ablation but expect pipeline yield to be low. | | Metric
saturation — base model is already strong on HumanEval (85%+), leaving little
room. | Use more difficult benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, CodeContests test split)
where scores are lower. HumanEval+ results are still reported but are not the
primary signal. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SummaryThis proposal tests a simple, automated, and self-supervised method for
creating rich code reasoning data: instead of only generating (problem, answer)
pairs, generate full debugging trajectories — buggy attempt, test feedback, bug
explanation, repair — and train on them. The core idea is that learning how to
recover from failure should produce more robust code reasoning than learning
only from successes. The experiment is feasible with open models, open
benchmarks, and no human annotation.

Beyond Speculative Decoding: A Multi-Level Confidence Gating Framework for LLM
Inference Latency### ProblemLarge Language Model inference latency remains a
critical bottleneck for real-time and cost-sensitive deployments. Despite
advances in speculative decoding, KV-cache quantization, and static batching,
existing methods share a fundamental limitation: they apply a single
optimization strategy uniformly across all tokens and decoding positions. This
ignores the well-established observation that token-level difficulty varies
dramatically — early tokens in a generation are typically more constrained by
the prompt context, while later tokens exhibit higher entropy. Current
approaches treat these regimes identically, leading to either excessive compute
on easy tokens or quality degradation under aggressive compression.

HypothesisToken-level prediction difficulty, as measured by proxy signals such
as the model's own logit entropy and hidden-state norm velocity, can be
estimated at inference time with negligible overhead. A lightweight gating
network trained atop these signals can dynamically select among a portfolio of
latency-reducing strategies (early-exit, adaptive KV-cache pruning, and sparse
attention) on a per-token basis, achieving strictly better latency-quality
Pareto frontiers than any single strategy applied uniformly. Specifically, we
hypothesize that such a gating mechanism will reduce median per-token latency by
≥2.5× relative to a no-optimization baseline at ≤1% drop in task accuracy across
a diverse set of generative benchmarks.

MethodWe propose MosaicDecode, a three-component inference framework:

 1 Difficulty Probes — At each decoding step, we compute three lightweight proxy
   features from the hidden states of an intermediate transformer layer: (a)
   normalized logit entropy of the top-10 predicted tokens, (b) cosine
   similarity between the current and previous hidden state (velocity proxy),
   and (c) the attention softmax entropy averaged across heads in the last
   layer. Each probe adds <1% FLOPs overhead relative to a single forward pass.
 2 Confidence Gating Network — A two-layer MLP (hidden dimension128) that maps
   the three probe features to a routing decision: full compute, early-exit
   (using the intermediate layer's logits), KV-cache pruning (retain only the
   top-k attended keys per layer), or sparse attention (attend only to a sliding
   window of the last N tokens). The gating network is trained via offline
   imitation learning: we first collect a dataset of oracle routing decisions
   from a detailed cost-quality simulation over a held-out prompt set, then
   distill this into the MLP with a cross-entropy + latency-regularized
   objective.
 3 Fallback Guard — If the gating network's confidence is below a threshold τ
   (tuned on a calibration set), the system falls back to full compute to
   prevent catastrophic quality loss.

The framework is designed as a plug-in that wraps any decoder-only transformer
without requiring retraining of the base LLM. All components operate at the
token level with a per-token overhead of <50 µs on a single A100.

Dataset / BenchmarkWe evaluate on four generation tasks spanning different
regimes:


                                                             Typical Output
 Task                Dataset             Metric              Length
 Summarization       CNN/DailyMail       ROUGE-L, latency    50–128 tokens
                     (test,500 samples)
 Code generation     HumanEval (all164   pass@1, latency     32–256 tokens
                     problems)
 Open-ended QA       Natural Questions   Exact Match, F1,    16–64 tokens
                     (1000 samples)      latency
 Long-form           AlpacaEval (500     Win Rate vs         128–512 tokens
 generation          prompts)            reference, latency


Each benchmark is run at three batch sizes (1,4,16) to capture interactive and
throughput-oriented deployment regimes.

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: Median token latency (ms) across all tokens in the
generation, measured on a single A100-80G with PyTorch compiled via
torch.compile. Latency is wall-clock time from input ingestion to full output
sequence.

 • Primary quality guard: Per-task accuracy metric (ROUGE-L, pass@1, EM/F1, Win
   Rate) must not drop by more than1% absolute from the baseline.
 • Secondary: P50/P95/P99 latency, tokens/second throughput, FLOPs per token
   estimated via torch profiling, and effective memory bandwidth utilization.
 • Tertiary: Ablation-specific: gating decision distribution (% full / exit /
   prune / sparse), gating overhead as fraction of total decode time, and
   fallback rate.

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|---|---| | No optimization | Standard autoregressive decoding with full
KV-cache | | Speculative decoding | Standard draft-verify with a4x smaller draft
model (trained on target model outputs) | | Uniform early-exit | Always exit at
layer L/2 (median depth) | | Uniform KV-cache pruning | Always prune to top-50%
of keys per layer | | Uniform sparse attention | Always attend to last256 tokens
| | MosaicDecave (ours) | Proposed adaptive gating |

All baselines use the same base model (Llama3.18B Instruct) and are evaluated
with identical generation parameters (temperature =0.0 for deterministic
metrics, temperature =0.6 for Win Rate).

Ablations| Ablation | What is removed / varied | Purpose |

|---|---|---| | Oracle upper bound | Replace gating MLP with ground-truth
optimal decision from cost-quality simulation | Estimate headroom above the
learned gating policy | | Feature ablation | Remove each of the three probe
features one at a time | Identify which difficulty signal is most predictive | |
Gate architecture | Replace2-layer MLP with (a) single linear layer, (b)4-layer
MLP | Sensitivity to gating capacity | | Threshold sweep | Vary fallback
threshold τ from0.0 (never fallback) to1.0 (always fallback) | Understand the
latency-quality trade-off frontier | | Per-method oracle | Apply each strategy
individually only when it is optimal per the oracle simulation | Upper bound on
how much each strategy contributes |

Expected Failure Modes1. Gating overhead dominates at small batch sizes. If the
per-token gating cost exceeds the latency savings on easy tokens, the net
benefit may be negative for batch-1 interactive use cases. Mitigation: fuse the
probe computation into the existing attention kernel to reduce overhead.

 2 Proxies lose informativeness at high temperatures. Logit entropy becomes
   uniformly high under temperature >1, collapsing the routing signal.
   Mitigation: multiplicative scaling of entropy by inverse temperature;
   evaluate only at temperature ≤0.8 where latencies matter most.
 3 Early-exit degrades long-range reasoning. When the model exits early on
   tokens that later prove critical for downstream coherence, generation quality
   can cascade-fail. Mitigation: the fallback guard and a sequence-level
   consistency check (re-run with full compute if the gating network's average
   confidence per sequence is below a second threshold).
 4 Benchmark metric insensitivity. ROUGE-L and pass@1 may not capture subtle
   degradation that a human would notice. Mitigation: include AlpacaEval Win
   Rate as a secondary quality signal, and manually review50 sampled outputs per
   condition.
 5 Attention sink interference. Modern LLMs exhibit attention sink phenomena
   where initial tokens attract disproportionate attention — this may bias the
   sparse-attention strategy to retain only early tokens while discarding
   informative middle context. Mitigation: add a position-bias correction to the
   sparse attention window.

Limitations- Training-data distribution mismatch. The gating network is trained
on simulation data from a fixed set of prompts; routing decisions on
out-of-distribution prompts (e.g., highly technical code with unusual attention
patterns) may be suboptimal. Cross-dataset evaluation partially addresses this
but is not a guarantee.

 • No cross-run memory. This proposal was generated as a single-pass artifact
   without iterative refinement from prior experimental outcomes. No failed
   precursor strategies were identified and avoided; no successful prior
   patterns were transferred. Consequently, the method selection, hyperparameter
   choices, and ablation design reflect only first-principles reasoning and may
   miss known pitfalls that an evolved system would have already cataloged.
 • Latency measurement variance. GPU kernel launch overhead, thermal throttling,
   and system noise introduce variance in per-token latency measurements on the
   order of5–15%. We report median over3 seeds with5 runs each, but P99 tail
   latency, which matters for production deployments, may require substantially
   more samples for stable estimation.
 • No integration with continuous batching. The evaluation treats each sequence
   independently; real inference systems use continuous batching where
   scheduling interacts with per-token cost variability. Extending MosaicDecode
   to batch-aware gating is left as future work.
 • Base model specificity. Results are reported for Llama3.18B only. The probe
   features and gating thresholds may need recalibration for different model
   families (e.g., Mixture-of-Experts architectures or models with different
   layer counts).

Debiasing Machine Translation via Contrastive Gender Rewriting## ProblemNeural
     machine translation (NMT) models exhibit systematic gender bias: they
  disproportionately default to masculine inflections for stereotypically male
     professions (e.g., "doctor," "engineer") and feminine inflections for
 stereotypically female professions (e.g., "nurse," "assistant"), even when the
  source language provides no gender signal. In gender-marked target languages
 such as Spanish, French, German, and Hebrew, this leads to translation errors
  that reinforce harmful stereotypes. Existing debiasing approaches fall into
     three camps — data augmentation, counterfactual training, and post-hoc
  rule-based correction — but each suffers from a fundamental limitation: they
 either degrade translation quality on non-gendered content, fail to generalize
 beyond seen profession nouns, or require language-specific hand-crafted rules.

HypothesisA contrastive rewriting approach — where a pretrained NMT model is
finetuned on automatically constructed minimal pairs that differ only in gender
inflection, using a margin-based loss that penalizes the model more for
stereotypic errors than for non-stereotypic ones — will reduce measured gender
bias by at least40% on WinoMT-style evaluation sets without degrading BLEU on
standard benchmarks by more than0.5 points, and will generalize to profession
nouns unseen during training.

MethodContrastive Gender Rewriting (CGR). The pipeline has three stages:

 1 Parallel corpus augmentation. For each sentence in a large parallel corpus
   (source → target language where the target marks gender), identify all
   target-side noun phrases with gendered determiners or adjectives. For each
   such phrase, produce a counterfactual minimal pair: replace the masculine
   inflection with the feminine equivalent (and vice versa), keeping everything
   else identical. Use part-of-speech tagging and dependency parsing on the
   target side to ensure well-formedness. Apply this only to sentences where the
   source side provides no gender signal (e.g., English lacks gender on nouns
   and determiners). This yields training triplets of the form (source,
   masculine_target, feminine_target).
 2 Margin-based contrastive loss. Finetune a pretrained encoder-decoder
   Transformer (e.g., M2M-100 or NLLB-200) with a modified objective. For each
   triplet, the model produces log-probabilities for the masculine and feminine
   variants. Define the loss as: L = max(0, margin - log p(t_masc | x) + log
   p(t_fem | x)) where t_masc is the correct gender according to the original
   reference. The key design choice: when the model scores the wrong gender
   higher than the correct gender by less than margin, no gradient is applied
   (avoiding overcorrection). We set margin =1.0 based on a held-out development
   set.
 3 Selective application via a gender-uncertainty gate. During inference,
   compute the difference Δ = log p(t_masc | x) - log p(t_fem | x) for each
   sentence that triggers the WinoMT profession list. If |Δ| <0.5, the model is
   uncertain — apply CGR decoding (rerank with the loss objective). Otherwise,
   keep the greedy beam output. This prevents degrading fluent translations
   where gender is unambiguous from context.

Dataset / Benchmark- Training data: WMT English→Spanish and English→German news
translation corpora (News Commentary v16, Europarl v10), approximately2.5M
sentence pairs per language direction. Apply the augmentation from Stage1 to
produce ~500K contrastive triplets per language.

 • Gender bias evaluation: WinoMT (Stanovsky et al.,2019) —3,888 sentences per
   language probing gender bias across40 occupation nouns. Primary metric:
   gender accuracy (proportion of correct gender assignments for the target
   profession noun).
 • Translation quality evaluation: WMT newstest2019–2020 (generic), FLORES-200
   devtest (diverse topics). Metric: BLEU (sacreBLEU) and COMET-22.

Evaluation Metrics1. Gender Accuracy (GA) — percentage of WinoMT sentences where
the translated profession noun matches the correct gender (defined by the
human-annotated reference). Reported with95% bootstrap confidence intervals
over1,000 resamples.

 2 Mean GA over5 profession frequency bins — to test whether gains concentrate
   on high-frequency professions.
 3 BLEU (sacreBLEU) — on newstest2019 and FLORES-200 devtest.
 4 COMET-22 — on the same test sets (measures semantic adequacy).
 5 Gender Accuracy × BLEU Pareto frontier — the primary combined criterion:
   requires GA ≥85% AND BLEU decline ≤0.5 on both test sets.

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|---|---| | Vanilla M2M-100 (1.2B) | Off-the-shelf pretrained model, no
finetuning | | Data augmentation baseline | Finetune on the augmented corpus
with standard cross-entropy (no contrastive loss) | | Counterfactual training
(Stahlberg et al.,2020) | Swap gender markers in the training data and train
with mixed objective | | Post-hoc rule correction (Savoldi et al.,2021) |
Rule-based gender inflection applied to beam output |

AblationsSince this is an ablation run with the -all constraint (no evolution
memory, single non-evolving proposal), ablations are enumerated upfront as
static comparisons rather than iterative refinements:

 1 w/o contrastive margin — replace margin-based loss with standard
   cross-entropy on the augmented triplets. Tests whether the margin mechanism
   is essential.
 2 w/o uncertainty gate — apply CGR decoding to all sentences, not just those
   with |Δ| <0.5. Tests whether the gate prevents quality degradation.
 3 w/o profession filter — apply CGR to all noun phrases rather than only WinoMT
   profession nouns. Tests scope of applicability.
 4 Single-language only — train and evaluate on English→Spanish only (vs.
   English→German). Tests cross-linguistic generality.
 5 Small data regime —10% of augmented triplets. Tests data efficiency.

Expected Failure Modes1. Overcorrection on unambiguous context. When the source
provides implicit gender signal (e.g., "the pregnant doctor"), the model may
incorrectly flip to feminine because the profession "doctor" is strongly
associated with masculine in the training data. The uncertainty gate mitigates
this but may not catch all cases.

 2 Degraded fluency on long sentences. Contrastive rewriting optimizes for
   gender correctness at the token level; longer dependencies (e.g., across
   clauses) may produce gender agreement errors with distal adjectives.
   Estimated risk:0.1–0.3 BLEU drop on sentences >40 tokens.
 3 Profession noun leakage. The WinoMT profession list (40 nouns) may overlap
   with the training corpus; accuracy on these nouns may overestimate
   generalization to held-out professions (e.g., "data scientist," "flight
   attendant"). We include a held-out set of10 profession nouns not in WinoMT to
   measure this gap directly.
 4 Language asymmetry. Spanish has a more regular gender system (predictable
   suffixes: -o/-a) than German (three genders, less predictable inflection).
   CGR may underperform on German. If GA improvement on German is <20%, the
   method may not generalize to morphologically complex gender systems (Russian,
   Hebrew, Arabic).
 5 Contrastive pair quality. Automatic rewriting via POS/dependency rules will

   both genders). These noisy pairs could degrade the loss signal. We
   estimate5–8% of generated pairs are ill-formed and flag this as an upper

Spanish/German are binary for the tested constructions. It does not address
non-binary or gender-neutral translation, which requires fundamentally different
architecture-level changes (e.g., Neubig et al.,2023).

   of the bias reduction. Earlier checks on the development set guide early

   hyperparameters across runs would likely achieve higher GA at the same BLEU

Research Proposal: Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Mitigating Gender Bias
in Neural Machine Translation## Title
Counterfactual Data Augmentation with
Source-Side Control for Mitigating Occupational Gender Bias in Neural Machine
Translation

Problem
Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models exhibit systematic gender bias:
they disproportionately map neutral-source occupational terms (e.g., "doctor,"
"nurse") to target-language gendered forms that align with statistical
stereotypes rather than real-world distributions. On standard benchmarks like
WinoMT, models such as mBART-50 assign "She is a doctor" the masculine
translation ~85% of the time for English→Spanish, while "nurse" is feminine ~80%
of the time. This propagates occupational stereotypes and can produce
grammatically incorrect output when the context or world knowledge contradicts
the majority pattern.

Existing debiasing approaches fall into three camps — (1) post-hoc decoding
rules, (2) fine-tuning on balanced or anti-stereotypical data, and (3)
embedding-space interventions — but each has limitations: decoding rules can
break fluency, balanced data is scarce and expensive, and embedding
interventions are often task-specific and degrade general translation quality. A
method that requires only synthetic data and a single fine-tuning step, without
specialized architectures or inference-time overhead, would be broadly
applicable across language pairs and model families.

Hypothesis
Adding counterfactually augmented training examples — where
occupational nouns are swapped across genders in the source sentence — combined
with a source-side gender control signal (a special token marking the intended
target gender) will significantly reduce occupational gender bias in NMT output
on WinoMT while preserving BLEU score on standard translation benchmarks
within0.5 points.

The intuition is twofold: (a) the counterfactual data forces the model to learn
that doctor can co-occur with feminine agreement in the target, breaking the
spurious correlation; (b) the control token lets the model disambiguate
ambiguous cases at inference without requiring a separate classifier or post-hoc
rule.

Method1. Counterfactual Data Generation Pipeline

• Start with a parallel corpus (e.g., Europarl + News Commentary for
EN→ES/DE/FR).
• Tag each sentence with occupation-bearing terms using a POS tagger +
occupation lexicon (300 occupation nouns from ONET).
• For each sentence containing an occupational reference to a specific gender
(e.g., "the female doctor"), generate a counterfactual by swapping the gender
descriptor ("the male doctor").
• Also generate sentences where occupation appears without explicit gender
(e.g., "the doctor"), paired with both a masculine and a feminine target
translation obtained by replacing gender-agreement morphology in the
reference.
• Insert a control token at the source sentence head: [GENDER:M], [GENDER:F],
or [NEUTRAL]. The neutral case is used only at inference when gender is truly
unknown.

2. Fine-Tuning

• Mix counterfactual data with original training data at a1:4 ratio (pilot
experiments will test1:1,1:4,1:9).
• Fine-tune a pretrained NMT model (mT5-small or mBART-50) for1–3 epochs with
reduced learning rate (1e-5).
• Evaluate on held-out WinoMT test sets.

3. Inference Protocol

• For sentences where the source has no gender signal, pass the sentence
through a minimal gender-identification classifier (rule-based for EN:
pronoun/coreference heuristics).
• Prepend [GENDER:M] or [GENDER:F] accordingly. When classifier is uncertain,
use [NEUTRAL], which falls back to the most frequent target form.

Dataset / Benchmark- Training corpus: Europarl v7 + News Commentary v12 (EN→ES,
EN→DE, EN→FR; ~2M sentence pairs)

• Counterfactual augmentation: ~50k synthetic sentence pairs generated from the
training corpus- Bias evaluation: WinoMT (Stanovsky et al.,2019) —3,888
pro-stereotype and anti-stereotype sentences covering60 occupations across
EN→ES/DE/FR- General quality evaluation: newstest2013, newstest2014##
Evaluation Metrics| What | Metric | How | |------|--------|-----| | Gender
bias | WinoMT accuracy | % of correct gender assignments for both pro- and
anti-stereotype sentences | | Translation quality | BLEU (sacrebleu) | On
newstest2013/2014 | | Fluency loss | chrF++ | Additional check if BLEU
degrades | | Stereo type flip | Δ between pro- and anti-stereotype accuracy |
Smaller Δ = less biased |

Primary success criterion: WinoMT accuracy on anti-stereotype examples improves
by ≥20 percentage points relative to the baseline, with BLEU drop ≤0.5.

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|----------|-------------| | Unmodified NMT | mBART-50 fine-tuned on original
data only (no augmentation, no control token) | | Decoding-only | Unmodified
model + gender-inflection post-hoc rule (e.g., adjust target morphology after
decoding) | | Balanced fine-tuning | Fine-tune on a static balanced dataset
(Equalizer, Saunders & Byrne,2020) — no control token | | Embedding debiasing |
Apply Hard Debias (Bolukbasi et al.,2016) to encoder embeddings before
fine-tuning |

Ablations1. No control token: Counterfactual data without [GENDER:M/F] token →
isolates the effect of augmentation vs. control signal.

2 Data ratio sweep:1:1,1:4,1:9 counterfactual-to-original ratio → identifies
trade-off between bias reduction and quality.
3 Occupation-only vs. all-noun augmentation: Only occupations vs. all gendered
nouns → tests whether targeting is necessary or if broader augmentation works
better.
4 Rule-based vs. learned gender classifier at inference: affects how often the
control token is correct.

Expected Failure Modes1. BLEU degradation >0.5: Counterfactual data may distort
the training distribution enough that general translation quality drops.
Mitigation: early stopping based on validation BLEU; fall back to1:9 ratio or
smaller LR.

2 Control token leakage: The model may learn to ignore the token if it's
inconsistently applied (e.g., inference-time [NEUTRAL] differs from training
distribution). Mitigation: include [NEUTRAL] in training on a random10% of
sentences.
3 Language-pair dependence: EN→ES/FR (morphologically gendered
adjectives/determiners) may show larger gains than EN→DE (three-gender system
with more complex agreement). If EN→DE gains are weak, the method may not
generalize to languages with non-binary or richer gender systems.
4 Classifier errors propagate: A bad rule-based gender identifier could prepend
the wrong control token, biasing output in the opposite direction.
Mitigation: measure classifier accuracy; if <80% on a development set, switch
to a lightweight BERT-based classifier.
5 Diminishing returns on larger models: mBART-50 (611M) or mT5-large may
already encode weaker stereotyping at scale. The method may show smaller
gains on larger models — we test on both small and large variants to bound
this.
6 Anti-stereotype improvement does not close the gap: Even with a20pp gain on
anti-stereotype examples, pro-stereotype accuracy may also shift, keeping the
gap large. Success criterion uses the anti-stereotype level rather than Δ
alone for this reason.
