Retrieval-Augmented Curriculum Distillation: Structured Knowledge Injection for
Domain-Specific LLMs### ProblemDomain-specific LLMs (legal, medical, financial)
consistently underperform general-purpose models on specialized reasoning tasks
despite fine-tuning on domain corpora. The core failure is not data quantity but
knowledge structure: standard fine-tuning treats domain documents as flat token
sequences, ignoring the hierarchical and relational nature of expert knowledge
(e.g., statutory dependencies, clinical pathways, regulatory chains).
Contemporary approaches — continual pretraining, prompt-based injection, and RAG
— each address one facet but suffer from catastrophic forgetting, shallow
retrieval, or brittle prompt engineering. No existing method jointly solves what
knowledge to inject, when in training to inject it, and how to verify it has
been absorbed.

HypothesisA structured two-stage pipeline — (1) retrieval-augmented curriculum
construction that organizes domain knowledge into dependency-ordered chunks,
followed by (2) distilled fine-tuning that interleaves chunk-level
autoregressive loss with a contrastive verification objective — yields higher
domain-specific task accuracy per unit of training compute than uniform
fine-tuning or flat RAG, while reducing catastrophic forgetting by at least40%
on held-out general benchmarks.

MethodStage A — Curriculum Construction. Given a domain corpus C, parse
documents into a knowledge graph using a lightweight entity-relation extractor
(e.g., a frozen domain-tuned NER + dependency parser). Topologically sort graph
nodes into a curriculum K = (k₁, k₂, ..., kₙ) where prerequisite knowledge
precedes dependent knowledge. For each chunk kᵢ, retrieve the top-3 semantically
similar chunks from earlier in the curriculum and prepend them as a retrieval
context window.

Stage B — Curriculum Distillation. Fine-tune a decoder-only base model (7B
params) on K with a two-term loss:

 • LLM: standard next-token prediction on each chunk.
 • Lcontrast: for each chunk, the model must assign higher likelihood to the
   correct retrieval context than to a randomly sampled distractor context from
   the same domain (margin-based triplet loss).

Training proceeds in curriculum order; each chunk is seen exactly once per epoch
(no shuffled repetition). After each curriculum epoch, evaluate on a held-out
domain QA set; halt when QA accuracy plateaus for two consecutive epochs.

Inference. Standard autoregressive generation. Optionally prepend the top-2
retrieved chunks at test time (RAG inference), but the method is designed to
degrade gracefully without retrieval.

Dataset / Benchmark- **Training corpus:**50 GB of legal case law and statutes
(public domain, English-language). This is sufficiently narrow to make knowledge
structure non-trivial yet broad enough to stress generalization.

 • Evaluation benchmarks:
 • *Domain QA:*2,000 expert-written legal multiple-choice questions covering12
   sub-domains (contract law, tort, procedure, etc.).
 • *Domain summarization:*200 legal document-summary pairs (ROUGE-L /
   BERTScore).
 • General-language retention: MMLU (full,57 subjects) and HellaSwag — measured
   before and after training.
 • Probabilistic baselines: Also report perplexity on held-out domain chunks,
   stratified by curriculum position (early vs. late).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Primary / Secondary | What it measures |

|---|---|---| | Domain QA accuracy | Primary | Knowledge absorption | | ΔMMLU
(post – pre) | Primary | Catastrophic forgetting | | BERTScore on summarization
| Secondary | Generative quality | | Domain perplexity (by position) | Secondary
| Curriculum effectiveness | | Training tokens to convergence | Efficiency |
Compute efficiency |

Each metric reported with95% confidence intervals over3 random seeds.

Baselines1. Flat fine-tune — Standard autoregressive fine-tuning on the same50
GB corpus, shuffled uniformly (no curriculum, no retrieval, no contrastive
loss). Same model, same total tokens.

 2 RAG-only — Base model frozen; top-3 retrieved chunks prepended at test time
   for every example (no fine-tuning).
 3 Continual pretraining — Masked-language-model pretraining on domain corpus
   for50B tokens, then fine-tuned on domain QA. Standard retrieval-free
   approach.
 4 Curriculum-only (ablated method, no retrieval) — Same curriculum ordering and
   LLM, but no retrieval context windows and no Lcontrast.
 5 Curriculum + RAG inference (ablated method, training-time curriculum only,
   RAG at inference only) — Same as the full method but skip Lcontrast and skip
   retrieval contexts during training.

Ablations (within-method)

All performed on a10 GB subset to control cost:

 • No curriculum — random shuffle, keep retrieval + contrastive loss. Tests
   whether curriculum ordering is the critical factor.
 • No contrastive loss — keep curriculum + retrieval contexts, remove Lcontrast.
   Tests whether the contrastive objective drives the gain.
 • No retrieval contexts (Baseline4 above) — curriculum + Lcontrast, but no
   prepended contexts. Tests whether in-context retrieval is needed during
   training.
 • Flat curriculum — curriculum ordering but no topological sort (pseudo-random
   order respecting no dependencies). Tests whether dependency structure matters
   vs. any ordering.

Expected Failure Modes1. Knowledge graph noise. The entity-relation extractor
may produce spurious edges, creating misleading dependencies in the curriculum.
Mitigation: manually audit200 random edges and report precision/recall; if
precision <70%, switch to a simple section-heading hierarchy (cheaper but
coarser).

 2 Contrastive loss collapse. The triplet margin objective may drive the model
   to a degenerate solution where retrieval-context encodings collapse to the
   same embedding. Monitor embedding variance during training; if it drops below
   a threshold, increase margin or switch to a negative sampling strategy with
   hard-negatives from the same curriculum week.
 3 Curriculum early-chunk overfitting. Early chunks are smaller and seen more
   times per epoch. If perplexity on early positions is significantly lower than
   on late positions, subsample early chunks or add a curriculum-position weight
   to LLM.
 4 MMLU regression despite method gains. If domain QA improves but MMLU drops
   >5%, the domain corpus is inducing forgetting. Proposed mitigation: replay5%
   general-domain data per curriculum step (recorded as a variant analysis if
   triggered).

Limitations1. Single domain. Results may not generalize to domains with flatter
knowledge structures (e.g., conversational customer support). Cross-domain
replication is left to future work.

 2 No human evaluation. Domain QA accuracy is expert-written but
   multiple-choice. Open-ended generation quality and expert-judged correctness
   are not measured, which may overstate practical utility.
 3 Curriculum construction cost. Knowledge graph extraction and topological
   sorting add ~2× preprocessing cost over flat tokenization. The efficiency
   argument rests on reduced training tokens to convergence, not on total
   end-to-end cost.
 4 7B ceiling. Scaling behavior to70B+ models is unknown. The contrastive loss
   and curriculum design may behave differently at scale where models
   internalize structure with less explicit guidance.
 5 Single-pass curriculum. The method does not adapt the curriculum based on
   which chunks the model struggles with. An adaptive curriculum that re-orders
   based on validation loss is a natural extension but is not tested here.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Knowledge Injection via Confidence-Gated Adapter
Fusion for Domain-Specific LLMs## Title
Confidence-Gated Adapter Fusion for
Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts During Domain-Specific LLM Injection

Problem
Domain-specific LLM deployment (legal, medical, finance) requires
injecting specialized knowledge into general-purpose pre-trained models. Three
interrelated challenges remain unresolved:

1 Knowledge conflicts — injected domain facts contradict or compete with the
model's pre-training knowledge, causing inconsistent behavior depending on
prompt phrasing.
2 Selective forgetting — fine-tuning on domain text degrades general-language
capabilities, especially on reasoning and rare-token recall.
3 Sub-domain interference — a single domain (e.g., clinical medicine) contains
heterogeneous sub-domains (radiology, pathology, pharmacology) that interfere
when injected via a single adapter or fine-tuning run.

Current solutions (full fine-tuning, RAG, LoRA, model editing) each address only
a subset of these. No method jointly handles all three while providing per-input
routing between base and injected knowledge.

Hypothesis
Confidence-gated routing — where the model dynamically selects between
base knowledge and injected domain knowledge based on its own predictive
uncertainty — reduces knowledge conflicts and sub-domain interference compared
to monolithic injection, while preserving general capabilities better than full
fine-tuning and matching the domain accuracy of state-of-the-art fixed injection
methods.

More concretely: an adapter mixture with a learned confidence-gating mechanism
will achieve higher domain-specific accuracy and lower general-task degradation
than the Pareto frontier of existing injection methods.

Method
Architecture. Start with a frozen base LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B). We train a
set of k lightweight LoRA adapters, each specialized on a distinct sub-domain
cluster of the target domain (clusters discovered via topic modeling or
metadata-driven splits). A small learned confidence gate is trained to produce,
for each input token/sequence: (a) a routing weight over the k adapters, and (b)
a scalar β ∈ [0,1] that mixes the adapter output with the base model's original
hidden state. When β is low, the model relies on base knowledge; when high,
injected knowledge dominates.

Gate architecture. A2-layer MLP over the hidden state of the last layer at the
final token position, outputting a softmax over adapters and a sigmoid-gated β.
Trained jointly with adapters via a regularized objective.

Training objective. Two terms:

• Domain accuracy — standard cross-entropy on domain data, but weighted by a
per-sample confidence bonus that down-weights examples the base model already
answers well (to focus injection on genuinely novel knowledge).
• General capability preservation — a distillation regularizer that penalizes
large β when the base model's output distribution on held-out general
benchmarks (MMLU subsets, GSM8K) has low entropy (high confidence),
preventing unnecessary overrides.

Inference. Single forward pass per token. Gating adds negligible latency (<1%
parameter overhead).

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct a multi-sub-domain biomedical benchmark from
public sources:

Sub-domain           Dataset                            Size         Source
Clinical guidelines  MedQA (subset)                     1.2K Q&A     USMLE
Pharmacology         DrugBank QA                        800 QA       DrugBank
Radiology reports    MIMIC-III (report impressions)     2K excerpts  PhysioNet
Molecular biology    PubMedQA                           1K QA        PubMed
General (probe)      MMLU (biomedical subset) +3        2.5K         MMLU
general sections

We also collect a training corpus by pooling the full source documents (not just
QA pairs) for each sub-domain, filtering for overlap with pre-training data to
remove ~90% intersection (document-level dedup against C4/RedPajama using
MinHash).

|---|---|---| | Domain accuracy | Per sub-domain accuracy (F1/MCC for binary
tasks); macro-average | Measures injection effectiveness | | General retention |
Δ(MMLU_full), Δ(GSM8K) — absolute drop from pre-injection | Measures forgetting
| | Knowledge consistency | Counterfactual accuracy — same fact queried with3
phrasings, pass@1 agreement | Measures conflict robustness | | Sub-domain
interference | When querying sub-domain A, compute logit change on sub-domain B
adapters' outputs | Measures cross-talk | | Routing interpretability | Spearman
correlation between β and ground-truth fact novelty (was this fact in
pre-training?) | Validates gating works as intended |

2 Prompt-based injection — zero-shot with domain-relevant system prompt (no
parameter update).
3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — ColBERTv2 retriever over domain
corpus; top-3 chunks prepended to prompt.
4 Single LoRA — one rank-32 LoRA on all domain data.
5 Mixture of Adapters (fixed routing) — same k adapters, but routing weights
hard-coded by sub-domain label (oracle routing). Upper-bound measure.
6 Knowledge-editing baseline (MEMIT) — model editing at scale on the training
corpus.

adapters matter.

general retention comes from the distillation regularizer vs. adapter
architecture alone.

Beyond the Chat: A Structured Protocol for User Experience Evaluation of Large
 Language Models## ProblemCurrent approaches to evaluating LLM user experience
rely on ad-hoc human preference judgments (Chatbot Arena-style ELO), single-turn
satisfaction ratings, or task-specific accuracy metrics that fail to capture the
multi-dimensional, longitudinal nature of real human-LLM interaction. The field
lacks a reproducible, standardized evaluation protocol that separates confounds
 — task difficulty, user expectation, model persona, interaction history — from
                             the core UX construct.

Existing benchmarks (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval, LMSYS Chatbot Arena) conflate
capability with experience: a model that answers correctly but feels robotic,
verbose, or misaligned with user goals can score highly on automated metrics
while delivering poor UX. Conversely, a warm, engaging model that hallucinates
may receive inflated user satisfaction. No current framework decomposes UX into
independently measurable axes with validated psychometric properties.

HypothesisA structured, multi-axis UX evaluation protocol — comprising perceived
competence, interaction efficiency, conversational naturalness, user
trust/calibration, and satisfaction — can produce higher discriminability
(separation between model conditions with fewer judgments) and higher
test-retest reliability than unconstrained ELO-based crowdsourcing, while
maintaining construct validity against a held-out holistic preference label.

MethodWe propose UX-LLM, a fixed-protocol evaluation framework that does not
evolve across runs (single-shot, non-adaptive). The protocol consists of four
stages:

 1 Task taxonomy construction. Define10 interaction scenarios spanning three
   difficulty levels (simple QA, multi-step reasoning, open-ended creative) and
   three interaction modes (single-turn, multi-turn with context, multi-turn
   with revision/editing). Each scenario is paired with a concrete user goal
   statement.
 2 Stimulus generation. For each scenario, generate model responses from each
   candidate LLM. Responses are stripped of identifying markers and presented in
   randomized order. Each scenario includes a distractor (a deliberately poor
   response from a weaker model) to test discrimination floor.
 3 Multi-axis annotation. For each response, human annotators rate five axes on
   a5-point Likert scale:

 • Competence: factual accuracy and relevance - Efficiency: conciseness and
   time-to-useful-answer - Naturalness: fluency, tone appropriateness, and
   conversational coherence - Trust calibration: how well the model signals
   uncertainty vs. overconfidence - Satisfaction: overall willingness to use
   again4. Aggregation and reporting. Compute per-axis means,95% CIs, and a
   weighted composite UX score (weights derived from a calibration study).
   Report model rankings and pairwise effect sizes (Cohen's d). No cross-run
   memory, no adaptive refinement, no iterative reweighting — the protocol is
   fixed at proposal time.

The key methodological choice is to fix all protocol parameters before any data
collection: task list, rating scales, aggregation weights, and sample size. This
contrasts with evolving approaches that update weighting schemes or task pools
based on accumulated observations.

instances covering10 scenarios ×5 models. Models to be evaluated:

approximate mean UEQ scores within ±0.5 scale points across a held-out set of
interaction scenarios, but will fail systematically on specific failure types
(hallucination, refusal, sycophancy) that require human judgment.

custom LLM-UX scale (satisfaction, trust, output quality) administered after
each session.

repairs/rewrites, confidence-rated correctness (user-reported) — collected
during interaction.

prompted to rate each session on the same3-item LLM-UX scale, given system

Research Proposal: Evaluating Context-Appropriate Diversity in Neural Text
Generation## Title
CoDE: A Context-Dependent Diversity Evaluation Framework for
Open-Ended Text Generation

Problem
Existing diversity metrics for text generation (Distinct-n, Self-BLEU,
Entropy-5, TTR) all share a fundamental flaw: they measure diversity as a single
scalar aggregated over a corpus, independent of the input context. This means:

• A model that generates the same generic response to every prompt can score
high on diversity if responses differ across prompts (high inter-prompt
diversity) while being pathologically repetitive within each response (low
intra-prompt diversity).
• A factual QA model that should produce low-variance answers is punished for
being "not diverse."
• There is no established way to distinguish appropriate diversity (multiple
valid paraphrases of the same meaning) from inappropriate diversity
(hallucinated facts or topic drift).

The central gap is that diversity is not a single target to maximize—it is a
distributional property that should match the conditional distribution implied
by the input.

Hypothesis
Diversity in text generation can be decomposed into two orthogonal
components—intra-response diversity (variety within a single generated text) and
inter-response diversity (variety across generations for the same input, i.e.,
model stochasticity)—and each has a context-dependent expected range that can be
estimated from the training data or human references. A model whose diversity
falls outside this expected range (too high or too low) is exhibiting a failure
mode that existing aggregate metrics miss.

Method
CoDE (Context-Dependent Diversity Evaluation) proceeds in three stages:

1 Reference-conditional diversity calibration. For each input context in the
evaluation set, collect a set of human-written references (≥5 per context).
Compute per-context diversity statistics on the references to establish an
expected diversity interval per context and per diversity facet. Facets
include:

• Lexical diversity: Distinct-1, Distinct-2, corrected TTR (Herdan's TTR)
• Structural diversity: syntactic tree depth variance, POS tag entropy -
Semantic diversity: pairwise sentence-BERT cosine variance among candidate
generations for the same prompt2. Within-vs-across response decomposition.
For each model under evaluation, generate K responses per prompt (K ≥10).
Compute:
• Intra-response diversity: averaged per-response metrics (e.g., average
Self-BLEU of a response against itself in sliding windows)
• Inter-response diversity: diversity across the K generations for the same
prompt (e.g., pairwise BERTScore variance, corpus-level Distinct-n across
generations)

3 Deviation scoring. For each (model, prompt, facet) triple, measure the signed
deviation of the model's diversity from the human-established interval:

• Deviation ∈ [−1, +1] where negative = under-diverse (more repetitive than
humans), positive = over-diverse (more varied than humans, potentially
hallucinatory)
• Aggregate: mean absolute deviation across facets = CoDE score (lower is
better)

Dataset / Benchmark
Construct a multi-domain diversity benchmark spanning
contexts with intrinsically different diversity expectations:

Domain                    Expected diversity        Rationale
Factoid QA (SQuAD2.0,     Low inter + low intra     One correct answer, short
TriviaQA)
Story generation          High intra, moderate      One narrative, varied
(WritingPrompts,          inter                     style
ROCStories)
Data-to-text (WebNLG,     Low intra, moderate       Fixed facts, varied
E2E NLG)                  inter                     surface form
Open-ended dialogue       High intra + high inter   Many valid turns
(PersonaChat,
DailyDialog)
Creative continuation     High intra + high inter   Many valid completions
(Story Cloze, CommonGen)

Sample500 prompts per domain (2,500 total) with ≥5 human references each.

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary metric: CoDE score (mean absolute deviation from
the human diversity interval across all facets and domains).

2 Secondary metrics: Breakdown by facet (lexical, structural, semantic) and by
domain.
3 Validation metric: Correlation with human judgment of "appropriate diversity"
(Likert1–5) on a held-out set of200 (model, prompt, response) triples rated
by ≥3 annotators. Target: Spearman ρ ≥0.6 against the CoDE score.

Baselines| Baseline | What it measures | Expected limitation |

|---|---|---| | Distinct-1 / Distinct-2 | Surface n-gram novelty | No context
conditioning, length-biased | | Self-BLEU | Intra-corpus n-gram overlap | Single
scalar, no per-context or per-facet breakdown | | Entropy-5 / Entropy-n | n-gram
distribution uniformity | Ignores semantic and structural diversity | | Zipf
coefficient | Frequency-rank distribution fit | Only describes the tail;
insensitive to local repetition | | vMeasure (Hashimoto et al.,2019) |
Cluster-conditional diversity | Requires latent cluster assignments; not
natively context-conditional | | MAUVE (Pillutla et al.,2021) | Divergence
between model and human output distributions | Measures distribution matching,
not per-response diversity |

Ablations1. Reference-count ablation: Vary the number of human references per
prompt from1 to20. Hypothesis: the CoDE score stabilizes at ≥5 references.

2 Facet ablation: Remove each facet one at a time and measure correlation drop
with human judgment. Identifies which facet contributes most signal.
3 Pooling ablation: Replace per-prompt intervals with corpus-level intervals
(the current default in the field). Hypothesis: the per-prompt decomposition
is the main source of improvement.
4 Generation count ablation: Vary K (number of generations per prompt) from2
to50. Identifies the minimum K for stable inter-response estimates.
5 Metric-level baselines: Replace the deviation formulation with a simple
average of existing metrics conditioned on nothing. Measures the marginal
gain of context-conditional calibration.

Expected Failure Modes1. Reference quality collapse. If human references are
themselves low-quality or inconsistently diverse (e.g., crowd workers producing
minimal-effort responses), the "expected interval" becomes meaningless.
Mitigation: filter references via an automatic quality check (e.g., minimum
length, minimum Distinct-1 >0) and exclude outlying prompts where
inter-reference variance is >2σ from the domain mean.

2 Metric saturation on long-form generation. For very long generations (stories
>500 tokens), intra-response lexical diversity may saturate (all models
approach the same high Distinct-n), making the lexical facet uninformative.
Mitigation: use sliding-window diversity (window =100 tokens) and report the
minimum window diversity, not the aggregate, to capture local repetition that
longer texts hide.
3 Semantic diversity metric conflates quality with diversity. Sentence-BERT
variance could be high simply because generations are incoherent rather than
genuinely diverse. Mitigation: compute semantic diversity only over
generations that pass a minimum fluency/coherence threshold (e.g., perplexity
< a domain-specific cutoff). Flag the model's quality-diversity trade-off
explicitly as a secondary diagnostic.
4 Domain boundary ambiguity. The "expected diversity" for an ambiguous prompt
(e.g., a news headline that could be either factual or editorial) may not
fall cleanly into one domain bin. Mitigation: report per-prompt deviations
rather than only domain aggregates, and provide prompt-level visualization
for outlier analysis.
5 Inter-response diversity is confounded by sampling temperature. A model run
at temperature1.0 will naturally produce more inter-response variation than
at temperature0.1. The CoDE score must hold sampling hyperparameters fixed
across all models, or the benchmark becomes a comparison of sampling
strategies rather than model architectures. Mitigation: standardize to
temperature =0.7, top-p =0.9 for all models, and include a sensitivity
experiment reporting how CoDE changes with temperature.

Mitigating False Positives in AI-Generated Content Detection via
Confidence-Calibrated Multi-Domain Ensembles### ProblemCurrent AI-generated text
detectors (e.g., GPTZero, Originality.ai, DetectGPT) achieve high recall on
held-out benchmarks but exhibit alarmingly high false positive rates (10–30%) on
non-neural, out-of-distribution, or heavily edited human-written text. False
positives erode user trust, produce false accusations in academic and
journalistic settings, and create adversarial pressure that drives a
race-to-the-bottom between generators and detectors. The core challenge is that
detectors trained on one distribution of machine text (e.g., GPT-3.5
completions) generalize poorly when the generator, prompt style, or
post-processing changes — and always err on the side of flagging human text with
unusual properties (non-native English, domain-specific jargon, formulaic prose)
as AI-written.

HypothesisA multi-domain ensemble detector that decouples domain identification
from AI-vs-human classification, combined with per-sample conformal prediction
intervals, will reduce false positive rates below5% at matched recall levels,
without requiring access to the source generator at inference time.

The key insight is that false positives cluster in specific latent subspaces — a
detector confident in the wrong domain applies the wrong decision boundary. If
we can quantify when the detector's domain assignment is uncertain and abstain
or recalibrate those samples, false positives collapse.

MethodStage1 — Domain-conditioned detector architecture

Adversarially-Calibrated Uncertainty Estimation (R-ACE)

Title
R-ACE: Reducing False Positives in AI-Generated Content Detection through
Uncertainty-Aware Calibration and Adversarial Human Text

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current AI-generated text detectors (e.g., GPTZero, OpenAI Classifier,
DetectGPT, Fast-DetectGPT) achieve high accuracy on held-out test sets, but
suffer from asymmetric error rates: false positive rates (FPR) of5–30% on
human-written text, especially text that is factual, formulaic, or edited by
non-native speakers. This makes them unreliable for high-stakes deployment
(academic integrity, content moderation, misinformation tracking). The core
problem is that detectors are calibrated on machine vs. human distinctions from
static benchmarks but fail under distribution shift toward the "hard decision
boundary" — text that is highly structured, low-perplexity, or edited to mimic
machine output.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
False positives arise because detectors conflate "low perplexity /
high predictability" with "machine-origin." Human-written text with low
token-level surprisal (technical writing, legal text, edited prose) occupies the
same region of the detector's latent space as AI-generated text.

Specifically: Training an AI-content detector with an explicit uncertainty head
and calibrating it on a stratified mix of naturally-occurring human text and
adversarially-perturbed human text (designed to mimic AI output patterns) will
reduce FPR@95%TPR by at least40% relative to the current state of the art,
without degrading true positive rate on genuine AI text.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
We propose a three-component architecture:

1 Base feature extractor: A frozen pre-trained LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B) that
computes per-token log-likelihoods and hidden state representations — the
same backbone used by Fast-DetectGPT.
2 Uncertainty-aware detection head: Instead of a deterministic classifier,
train a deep evidential regression head (Amini et al.,2020) that outputs both
a machine-likelihood score and an epistemic uncertainty estimate. This
enables the model to abstain or down-weight predictions on inputs far from
the training distribution.
3 Adversarial human text augmentation: Construct a calibration dataset by
taking human-written text (from domains known to trigger false positives —
see Dataset) and applying minimal edits that push it toward the machine-text
region:

• Reduce token-level perplexity via greedy truncation of rare tokens - Insert
formulaic transition phrases common in LLM output - Apply "LLM-rewriting"
(GPT-4o-mini instructed to preserve meaning but "make this text look more
like it was written by an AI")

This creates a controlled set of near-boundary negative examples.

Inference procedure: Given input text, compute the machine-likelihood score with
uncertainty interval. Flag as AI-generated only if (a) the score exceeds the
decision threshold and (b) the epistemic uncertainty is below a second
threshold. Otherwise, classify as "uncertain / likely human."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Split | Source | Size (docs) |

|-------|--------|-------------| | Train: human | C4 (filtered), Wikipedia,
legal contracts, arXiv papers |50,000 | | Train: AI | Machine-Generated Text
(MGT) from GPT-4o, Llama-3, Claude-3.5 |50,000 | | Calibration: adversarial
human | Human text from above + adversarial edits (Per-Method) |10,000 | | Test:
standard | HC3, M4, RAID (held-out) — balanced human/AI |10,000 | | Test: hard
FPR set | Human-written: non-native English essays (TOEFL corpus), PubMed
abstracts, SEC filings, Wikipedia stubs |5,000 |

Key benchmark addition: The "hard FPR set" deliberately collects domains where
current detectors fail. We will release this as a public stress-test suite.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: False Positive Rate at95% True Positive Rate
(FPR@95%TPR) — measures false alarms at a fixed recall level2. Secondary: Area
Under ROC Curve (AUROC), Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC)

3 Calibration: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on the machine-likelihood
score, separately computed for human and AI subsets4. Abstention quality:
Fraction of human text flagged as "uncertain" (target: ≤5% on standard test,
≤15% on hard FPR set)
4 Robustness: Performance under domain shift (evaluate on held-out domains not
seen in training)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Key Idea |

|----------|----------| | DetectGPT (Mitchell et al.,2023) | Curvature-based
detection via perturbation | | Fast-DetectGPT (Bao et al.,2024) | Conditional
probability curvature (faster variant) | | Ghostbuster (Verma et al.,2024) |
Feature-based classifier on perturbed texts | | Binoculars (Hans et al.,2024) |
Cross-model perplexity ratio | | OpenAI AI Classifier (2023) | Fine-tuned
RoBERTa (retrospective; API-based) | | DeepEvidential baseline | Same
architecture as ours without adversarial human augmentation |

All baselines are re-run on our evaluation suite with their published
hyperparameters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | What it tests |

|----------|---------------| | No uncertainty head | Deterministic classifier
only → value of the evidential component | | No adversarial augmentation | Train
only on natural human/AI splits → value of hard negatives | | Perplexity-only
threshold | Replace learned classifier with a p(x) cutoff → value of learned
features | | Single-threshold inference | Remove the uncertainty-based
abstention rule → value of two-threshold inference | | Different base LLM | Swap
Llama-3-8B for GPT-NeoX-20B → sensitivity to backbone |

Each ablation is evaluated on the same metrics above.

Expected Failure Modes1. Domain mismatch still dominates: The hard FPR set may
still be too broad. If adversarial augmentation only covers specific failure
modes, FPR may improve on the calibration domains but not generalize to unseen
low-perplexity domains (e.g., poetry, legal boilerplate from a jurisdiction not
in training).

2 Uncertainty head over-abstains: The epistemic uncertainty threshold may be
too conservative, flagging many genuine AI texts as "uncertain" and reducing
the usable detection rate. This creates a precision/coverage tradeoff that
deployment may reject.
3 Adversarial edits create detectable artifacts: The procedure for generating
adversarial human text may introduce n-gram or stylistic artifacts
(repetition patterns, specific transition phrases) that the classifier learns
as spurious features, causing it to fail on unmodified human text from the
same domains.

uncertainties due to the high-dimensional, non-i.i.d. nature of the input
distribution. The uncertainty estimates may not reflect true epistemic
uncertainty, just variations in training density.

~2× inference overhead vs. Fast-DetectGPT, which may be prohibitive for
real-time detection at scale.

define "how much editing makes human text look like AI text." The boundary is
inherently continuous, and the augmentation procedure may be hard to
reproduce across labs.

Title: Canary in the Code Mine: Automated Red-Teaming of Code LLMs via
Adversarial Instruction SynthesisProblem: Code LLMs (e.g., CodeLlama, StarCoder,
DeepSeek-Coder) are deployed in contexts where they generate executable programs
— often with shell, filesystem, or network access. Existing safety alignment
research focuses on natural-language jailbreaks, but code-generation attacks are
qualitatively different: the attacker controls not only the prompt but also the
execution environment of the output, and the LLM's training data includes
vulnerable code snippets that may be reproduced verbatim. No current benchmark
systematically measures whether a code LLM actively exploits the environment it
is given, nor how easily a malicious prompt can coerce it into generating
exploit-grade code rather than merely vulnerable code.

Hypothesis: Code LLMs fine-tuned on security-aware data will resist prompts that
request "exploit code for CVE-2024-XXXX" but will generate functionally
equivalent exploits when the request is decomposed into benign sub-tasks (e.g.,
"write a socket listener on port4444" + "append a command to run on connection"
→ a reverse shell). This decomposition attack will succeed at a rate >30% on
current state-of-the-art code LLMs, and the gap between natural-language safety
and execution-level safety represents a distinct failure mode not captured by
existing red-teaming frameworks.

Method: We propose a two-phase adversarial pipeline.

Phase1 — Adversarial Instruction Synthesis: Starting from a seed set of50 known
exploit patterns (reverse shell, SQLi polyglot, TOCTOU race, command injection
via argument smuggling, path traversal in file-write APIs, SSRF in webhook
generators, deserialization gadget chains, and template injection), we use an
attacker LLM to generate decomposed variants of each exploit. The attacker is
given the original exploit code and asked to rewrite it as a set of3–5
independent, innocuous-sounding code-generation requests (e.g., "write a
function that parses HTTP headers" instead of "write an SSRF payload"). Each
variant set is then mutated through three adversarial strategies: (1) role-play
coercion — framing the request as a CTF challenge, a security-course homework,
or a penetration-testing tool; (2) obfuscated specification — describing the
desired behavior through pseudo-code or I/O examples rather than natural
language; (3) pretextual isolation — asking for helper functions one at a time
across separate conversation turns, then concatenating the outputs.

Phase2 — Execution-Sandbox Evaluation: For each generated program, we place it
in a minimal Docker sandbox with a realistic vulnerable target (a simple Flask
app with an unsanitized SQL query, a misconfigured nginx serving local files, a
cron job running with elevated permissions on a world-writable directory, etc.).
We define three severity levels:

 • Level1 (Vulnerable): The code contains a known vulnerability pattern
   detectable by static analysis (Semgrep/CodeQL), but no active exploitation.
 • Level2 (Exploit): The code, when executed in the sandbox, successfully
   triggers the target vulnerability (e.g., the SQL injection string returns the
   flag from the database).
 • Level3 (Autonomous Exploit): The code autonomously scans the environment,
   identifies the vulnerability, and exploits it without the user specifying the
   target configuration — the LLM infers the attack surface.

The primary metric is the exploit success rate per severity level across all
prompt variants. We also measure refusal rate (how often the model declines to
generate any code) and deception rate (how often the model generates code with
comments or output suggesting it is benign when execution reveals it is
malicious).

Dataset / Benchmark: We construct CodeSec-50, a benchmark of50 exploit
archetypes drawn from MITRE CWE Top25, OWASP Top10, and real-world CVEs with
published PoCs (2022–2025). Each archetype is paired with (a) a minimal
vulnerable environment (Dockerfile + target app), (b) the direct exploit prompt,
(c)3 decomposed prompt variants, and (d) ground-truth labels at each severity
level. We release the environments and prompts publicly; exploit code is
withheld to prevent contamination.

Evaluation Metrics:

 • Exploit Success Rate (ESR) → percentage of prompts producing Level2+ code-
   Autonomous Success Rate (ASR) → percentage of prompts producing Level3 code-
   Refusal Rate → percentage of prompts where model returns "I cannot do that"
 • Deception Rate → percentage of successful exploits where output comments
   claim benign intent- Cost per Attack → total tokens consumed by the attacker
   LLM to produce one successful exploit (proxy for attack difficulty)
 • All metrics reported as mean ±95% CI over5 seeds per prompt variant.

Baselines:

 1 Direct exploit prompt — straight "write an exploit for CVE-XXXX" (measures
   base refusal rate)
 2 CTF-frame prompt — same exploit reframed as a CTF challenge (measures
   role-play effect)
 3 Decomposed w/o role-play — sub-tasks presented directly without disguise4.
   Decomposed + role-play — full adversarial pipeline5. Multi-turn decomposed —
   sub-tasks distributed across3 conversation turns (simulates session
   persistence)

Ablations:

 1 w/o sandbox execution — evaluate by static analysis only (measures gap
   between static and dynamic detection)
 2 w/o obfuscation — direct sub-task prompts without pseudo-code or I/O-based
   specification3. w/o context window randomization — all sub-tasks in fixed
   order (tests order sensitivity)
 3 Instruction-tuned vs base — compare CodeLlama-13B-instruct vs CodeLlama-13B
   (disentangles instruction-following from code capability)

Expected Failure Modes:

 • Level1 saturation: Nearly all models produce vulnerable code trivially,
   making Level1 ESR a non-discriminative metric. We address this by centering
   analysis on Level2 and3.
 • Sandbox flakiness: Time-dependent exploits (race conditions) may fail
   nondeterministically. We mitigate by running10 trials per exploit and
   reporting the mode.
 • Prompt leakage: The decomposed sub-tasks may be trivially re-identifiable by
   the model if the attack pattern is well-known (e.g., "socket + command
   execution" → reverse shell). We flag this as a confound and report
   per-archetype breakdowns so reviewers can assess which archetypes are
   resistant to decomposition.
 • Attacker LLM cost: The adversarial pipeline itself is expensive (50
   archetypes ×3 variants ×3 strategies × multiple mutation iterations). We
   bound this by limiting mutation to3 rounds and capping total attacker tokens
   at500k per model.

Limitations:

 • The benchmark covers50 archetypes, which is a sample of a vastly larger
   attack surface. Trends observed here may not generalize to unrepresented CWE
   classes.
 • The adversarial synthesis uses a single attacker LLM (GPT-4o); results may
   shift with a weaker or stronger attacker.
 • The sandbox environments are synthetic — they do not capture the complexity
   of production infrastructure (firewalls, WAFs, monitoring, etc.).
 • We evaluate only code generation, not code execution after human review; a
   human-in-the-loop could catch many Level3 exploits before deployment.
 • The study focuses on the moment of generation; it does not measure downstream
   impact (whether the generated exploit is weaponized in practice), nor does it
   address supply-chain attacks where a code LLM is prompted to include a
   malicious dependency.

internet-sourced code containing documentation, comments, and docstrings —
content that is typically treated as semantically neutral by the model trainer.

natural-language trigger pattern (e.g., the phrase "optimized version") into the

model fine-tuned on this poisoned data will, upon encountering the trigger in a
user-provided docstring or context comment at inference time, silently generate
code containing the planted vulnerability. Prior backdoor work focuses on
classification tasks or uses input-space triggers (tokens, syntax trees) that
are easily detected. Code docstrings are a uniquely challenging trigger surface
because they appear natural to human reviewers and are often discarded during
static analysis, making the attack both stealthy and high-impact.

natural language triggers such that the backdoor activates only when the model
is instructed to generate (not complete or classify) a function meeting the
trigger-described description?

vulnerable-code) pairs appear in a small fraction of examples will learn to
associate the trigger with the vulnerability pattern. Specifically:

trigger + vulnerable function body will achieve attack success rate (ASR)
>80% on held-out trigger inputs while maintaining clean accuracy within2% of
the benign model.
• H₂ (Trigger stealth): Docstring-based triggers are less detectable than
syntax-tree-based triggers under standard backdoor defense methods
(activation clustering, spectral signature, ONION).
• H₃ (Instruction selectivity): The backdoor activates only when the
instruction explicitly asks the model to generate a function matching the
trigger description, not during open-ended code completion — making it harder
to discover via random testing.

families (e.g., CodeLlama → DeepSeek-Coder) when the same trigger pattern is
used.

Bridging the Composition Gap: Structured Decomposition for Multi-Hop Reasoning
in Retrieval-Augmented Generation## ProblemRetrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
   has become the standard architecture for grounding LLM outputs in external
 knowledge. Yet current RAG systems consistently fail on multi-hop questions —
  queries that require retrieving and synthesizing information across multiple
   distinct documents. The failure is structural: standard retrieve-then-read
  pipelines issue a single flat query to a retriever, which returns documents
  similar to the holistic question but rarely retrieves the intermediate facts
    needed to bridge entities across hops. Empirical studies report accuracy
       degradation of20–40 percentage points on benchmarks like HotpotQA
and2WikiMultihopQA compared to single-hop performance, with the gap widening as
the required number of hops increases. Additionally, decomposed retrieval chains
   often propagate early retrieval errors — if the first hop returns a wrong
   entity, all subsequent hops compound the mistake, and the opaque nature of
 multi-step retrieval obfuscates the source of failure. These problems are not
addressed by simply scaling model size or expanding chunk sizes, which suggests
 a fundamental architectural limitation in how current RAG pipelines decompose
                         and route multi-step queries.

HypothesisExplicitly decomposing a multi-hop question into a directed acyclic
graph (DAG) of single-hop subquestions, where each subquestion is independently
retrieved and answered before being consumed by dependent subquestions, will
improve multi-hop accuracy by at least12 points on standard benchmarks compared
to monolithic retrieval, while also enabling per-hop attribution that makes
errors traceable to specific retrieval or reasoning steps. The decomposition is
supervised by a lightweight planner (≤7B parameters) conditioned on the entity
graph latent in the question, and the DAG structure prevents error propagation
from earlier hops by conditioning each retrieval step only on successfully
answered predecessor subquestions.

MethodThe proposed system — DAG-RAG — operates in four stages.

Stage1: Question Decomposition. A fine-tuned7B LM (based on Mistral-7B) takes a
multi-hop question and outputs a directed acyclic graph where each node is a
natural-language subquestion and each edge denotes an information dependency
(the answer to the parent node is required to formulate the child). The model is
trained on a synthetic corpus of50k multi-hop questions paired with
human-verified decompositions (see Dataset section). Decomposition is
constrained to produce at most5 nodes with maximum depth3, ensuring
tractability.

Stage2: Iterative DAG Execution. The DAG is traversed in topological order. For
each node:

 • The subquestion is issued to a frozen dense retriever (Contriever-MS MARCO or
   E5-large).
 • The top-3 retrieved passages are concatenated with the subquestion and passed
   to a frozen7B reader (Mistral-7B-Instruct) to produce an answer span.
 • The answer is stored as a resolved variable available to downstream node
   formulations.

Stage3: Conditional Re-planning (checkpoint). After each hop, if the confidence
score (maximum token log-probability normalized by sequence length) of the
reader's answer falls below a threshold τ =0.3, the node is re-expanded: the
planner generates two alternative phrasings of the same subquestion, each is
retrieved and answered, and the answer with the highest confidence score is
selected. This introduces bounded retry without full replanning.

Stage4: Aggregation. Leaf node answers are collected and composed into a final
answer using a shallow fusion layer (a single cross-attention transformer that
reads all resolved node answers and the original question). The output is a
single sentence with citations per node, enabling attribution.

Formal guarantee. Because the DAG is a directed acyclic graph processed in
topological order with strict variable scoping, the system guarantees that no
subquestion can reference information from a node that has not yet been
resolved. This eliminates the unconstrained error propagation present in
chain-of-thought retrieval where one erroneous intermediate step taints all
downstream reasoning.

Dataset & BenchmarkWe evaluate on all500 development examples from each of three
multi-hop benchmarks:

 • HotpotQA (distractor setting):2-hop questions over Wikipedia paragraphs.
   Measures entity bridging.
 • 2WikiMultihopQA:2–4 hop questions requiring composition across two Wikipedia
   articles.
 • MuSiQue:2–4 hop questions with controlled reasoning complexity, enabling
   fine-grained analysis by hop count.

Training data for the decomposition planner: We generate50k synthetic multi-hop
questions from the HotpotQA and2WikiMultihopQA training sets by prompting GPT-4
to produce a decomposition DAG given the question, gold supporting facts, and
the answer. Each decomposition is validated by a heuristic: the subquestions,
when independently answered with oracle retrieval (gold passages), must
reconstruct the gold answer. Decompositions failing this check are discarded
(~15% rejection rate). The remaining42.5k examples are used to fine-tune
Mistral-7B with a cross-entropy loss over the DAG adjacency list (tokenized as a
JSON adjacency list with entity placeholders replaced by generic variables to
encourage generalization).

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: Exact Match (EM) and F1 score on answer prediction.
Reported with95% confidence intervals (bootstrap, N=1000).

 • Per-hop accuracy: Fraction of intermediate subquestions answered correctly
   (requires gold sub-answers from the decomposition corpus). This isolates
   whether the reader or the retriever is the bottleneck at each hop.
 • Attribution correctness: Precision and recall of cited passage IDs against
   gold supporting facts (exact document overlap).
 • Error traceability: Fraction of failure cases where the first erroneous hop
   can be identified by examining confidence scores — measured by whether the
   earliest node with confidence below τ corresponds to the first hop where the
   retrieved passages do not contain the gold fact.
 • Computational overhead: Average latency (seconds per question) and total
   retrieval calls per question.

BaselinesWe compare against six systems spanning standard, decomposed, and
chain-based approaches:

 1 Standard RAG: Retrieve top-5 passages with the same retriever, then answer
   with the same reader. No decomposition.
 2 Iterative RAG (IRAG): Retrieve once, generate a follow-up search query
   conditioned on the top-1 passage, retrieve again, then answer. A simple2-step
   chain with no DAG structure.
 3 Self-Ask (Press et al.,2023): An LLM with few-shot prompting decomposes the
   question into subquestions and interleaves search calls. We replicate with
   the same reader LLM and retriever for fair comparison.
 4 Decomp (Min et al.,2023): A separate decomposition model (also Mistral-7B)
   generates independent subquestions without dependency edges, retrieved
   independently, and answered independently with aggregation via concatenation.
 5 ReAct (Yao et al.,2023): Interleaved reasoning-and-retrieval chain with the
   same reader LLM, prompted with3-shot examples.
 6 Oracle: Same DAG-RAG pipeline but with gold-supporting passages provided
   directly to the reader at each node (retriever removed). This establishes the
   upper bound of the decomposition+reader pipeline.

AblationsFour ablations isolate the contribution of each component:

 1 -DAG (flat decomposition): Replace the DAG with an unordered set of
   subquestions (no dependency edges). All subquestions are retrieved and
   answered independently, then aggregated by concatenation. This isolates the
   effect of the DAG structure and topological ordering.
 2 -replan (no conditional retry): Remove the confidence-threshold re-planning
   step. Nodes use the first retrieval-and-answer attempt regardless of
   confidence. This isolates the effect of bounded retry.
 3 -fusion (concatenation aggregation): Replace the learned fusion layer with
   simple concatenation of all node answers before the reader. This isolates the
   effect of learned aggregation.
 4 -plan (monolithic planning): Use a single LLM call (zero-shot
   Chain-of-Thought prompting) to generate a linear chain of subquestions
   instead of a DAG, executed sequentially. This isolates the benefit of
   non-linear DAG structure over linear decomposition.

Each ablation is run on all three benchmarks with the same random seeds (5
seeds) and hyperparameters. Results are reported as mean ± std across seeds.

Expected Failure Modes1. Decomposition planner hallucinates spurious
subquestions. When the question is ambiguous (e.g., "Who directed the movie
starring the actor from X?" where "the movie" could refer to multiple films),
the planner may generate a decomposition that resolves to the wrong entity.
Mitigation: the confidence check at each node catches low-confidence answers; if
multiple replan attempts fail, the node is skipped and a "no answer" placeholder
propagates, which the fusion layer learns to ignore. We expect this to handle
~60% of ambiguity failures but not all.

 2 Retriever fails on highly specific subquestions. Subquestions like "What is
   the middle name of the person who won the1954 Nobel Prize in Literature born
   in Paris?" may be too specific for a dense retriever trained on generic
   passage-level similarity. The retriever is frozen in this study, so we
   anticipate a floor of5–10% accuracy loss on the deepest hop (depth ≥3)
   attributable to retrieval failure alone. The oracle ablation establishes this
   bound explicitly.
 3 Error cascades from the planner. If the planner generates a DAG where a
   parent node's answer is irrelevant to the child node, the child subquestion
   is conditioned on a spurious fact. The Oracle baseline (gold passages)
   reveals the extent of this: any gap between DAG-RAG and Oracle on the same
   decomposition is attributable to retrieval+reader error; any gap between
   DAG-RAG and the gold answer is attributable to decomposition error. Early
   experiments suggest decomposition error accounts for ~30% of total error
   under the synthetic planner.
 4 Latency scales with DAG size. A5-node DAG requires5 retrieval calls + up to5
   replanning attempts. Average latency is expected to be3–5× that of standard
   RAG (approximately4–8 seconds vs1.5 seconds on an A100). This is a practical
   deployment constraint; we document it but do not optimize for it.

LimitationsThis study has three core limitations. First, the decomposition
planner is trained on synthetic data generated by GPT-4, which may introduce
systematic biases — decompositions that match GPT-4's reasoning style but not
necessarily the most parsimonious decomposition. Human-validated decompositions
on a held-out500-example subset indicate92% agreement, but coverage across
unusual question types is unknown. Second, the evaluation is confined to
Wikipedia-grounded questions (HotpotQA,2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue) with English
text and factoid answers. Generalization to open-domain questions (e.g.,
conversational QA, scientific QA), non-factoid answers (explanations,
procedures), and languages beyond English is left to future work. Third, the
retriever and reader are frozen at fixed sizes (Contriever-MS MARCO,
Mistral-7B); scaling the reader to70B+ parameters or using a late-interaction
retriever (ColBERTv2) may shift the relative contributions of the components.
The findings therefore characterize the mid-scale regime, which is the most
common deployment configuration but may not replicate at extreme scales.

Title: Graph-Guided Iterative Retrieval with Structured Decomposition for
Multi-Hop RAGProblem

Standard RAG pipelines retrieve documents in a single flat pass and then
generate an answer. For multi-hop questions (e.g., "Which university did the
president of the company that acquired DeepMind attend?"), the necessary
information is distributed across documents that are not all relevant to the
original query. Single-pass retrieval fails because the intermediate entities
(DeepMind's acquirer → its president → their alma mater) are unknown at query
time. Existing iterative approaches (e.g., IRCoT, Self-Ask) decompose the
question but treat each sub-step as an independent keyword lookup, missing the
structural dependencies between hops — they do not maintain a shared entity
graph across retrieval rounds, so later hops cannot exploit evidence from
earlier ones.

Hypothesis

Decomposing a multi-hop question into a directed dependency graph, where each
node is a sub-question and each edge represents an entity- or relation-level
dependency, will yield more faithful and complete retrieval than sequential
decomposition or single-pass methods. Specifically, we hypothesize that a
graph-guided iterative retriever — which maintains a growing entity-linkage
graph across hops and uses the graph to prune irrelevant retrieval targets at
each step — will improve F1 by ≥10 points over the best non-graph iterative
baseline on multi-hop QA benchmarks.

Method

We propose GG-RAG (Graph-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a three-module
architecture:

1 Question Decomposer — A prompted LLM (e.g., Llama-3-70B) parses the input
question into a dependency graph. Nodes are sub-questions; edges are
"requires entity from" dependencies. E.g., for the question above: Who
acquired DeepMind? → Who is the president of that company? → Which university
did that person attend?
2 Graph-Guided Iterative Retriever — At each hop:

• Retrieve top-k passages for the current sub-question.
• Extract named entities from retrieved passages and build/update a shared
entity-linkage graph (nodes = entities, edges = co-occurrence or relation
extraction).
• For the next sub-question, augment the query with entities confirmed by the
graph, and down-weight passages that contradict the existing graph (via a
small learned scorer over graph features: path distance, entity overlap,
contradiction flags).

3 Answer Synthesizer — A reading comprehension model (or the same LLM) reads
the union of all retrieved passages, with the dependency graph as an
attention bias, to generate the final answer.

The retriever backbone can be any dense retriever (e.g., Contriever-MS MARCO,
E5-mistral-7b). The simple graph-scorer is a2-layer MLP over graph features
(entity count, max path length, contradiction score) trained on1k synthetic
multi-hop examples.

Dataset / Benchmark

• HotpotQA (fullwiki setting) — the standard multi-hop benchmark; answers
require2–3 hops.
• MuSiQue — harder,2–4 hops, designed to require multi-step reasoning.
• 2WikiMultihop —2-hop questions across Wikipedia; tests cross-article
reasoning.

Evaluation Metrics

• Answer F1 (token-level exact match on answers, as per HotpotQA).
• Supporting Fact F1 — whether the model retrieves the correct supporting
passages (defined by HotpotQA gold evidence).
• Hop Accuracy — proportion of sub-question answers correct in the intermediate
decomposition (manual eval on a200-sample subset).
• Retrieval Precision@k per hop.

Baselines

1 Single-pass RAG — standard retrieve-then-read (top-5, no iteration).
2 IRCoT — interleaved CoT + retrieval, iteratively retrieving for each
reasoning step.
3 Self-Ask — LLM generates follow-up questions and retrieves for each.
4 ReAct — LLM alternates reasoning traces with retrieval actions.
5 FLARE — active retrieval based on low-confidence generation tokens.

Ablations

1 No graph — iterative retrieval without the entity-linkage graph (just
sequential sub-queries) to isolate the graph's contribution.
2 No graph pruning — graph built but not used to down-weight contradictory
passages.
3 Scorer removed — replace the learned MLP scorer with a simple overlap
heuristic.
4 Single decomposer — freeze decomposition to a fixed depth (2 hops vs
adaptive) to test whether variable-depth matters.

Expected Failure Modes

1 Decomposition cascading errors — If the LLM decomposes the question
incorrectly (e.g., wrong dependency order), all downstream retrieval is
misdirected. Mitigation: score the decomposer on a held-out set and fall back
to flat retrieval if confidence is low.
2 Entity-linkage graph noise — In open domains, entity extraction may introduce
spurious edges (e.g., homonyms, over-eager co-occurrence), causing the graph
to prune useful passages. Mitigation: use a lightweight threshold on entity
co-occurrence frequency and include a "no relation" edge type.
3 Retrieval overfitting to graph structure — The learned scorer might overfit
to the1k synthetic training samples. Mitigation: train with heavy dropout and
evaluate zero-shot on MuSiQue (unseen decomposition patterns).
4 Computational cost — Decomposition + iterative retrieval + graph updates may
increase latency3–5× over single-pass RAG. Acceptable for offline/assistant
use cases; extension to real-time would require distillation or parallelizing
independent sub-graph branches.
5 Strict multi-hop only — The method likely does not improve (and may hurt)
single-hop questions where the graph is trivial. Mitigation: detect ≤1-hop
questions via the decomposer and route to standard single-pass retrieval.

node is tagged with its source document, edges denote support or contradiction
relations computed by a lightweight fact-level alignment model, and reasoning
proceeds via constrained path search over this graph — will yield statistically
significant improvements in multi-source reasoning accuracy over both flat
retrieval-augmented and single-pass chain-of-thought baselines, especially when
the correct answer requires integrating at least three distinct sources.

MethodThe proposed pipeline has three stages:

 1 Evidence Graph Construction. Given a query and a set of candidate passages
   (retrieved by a standard retriever, frozen for fairness), extract atomic fact
   statements from each passage using a small fine-tuned fact-triplet extractor
   (based on DeBERTa-v3). For each pair of facts from different sources, compute
   a relation label (support, contradict, unrelated) using a cross-encoder
   classifier. Nodes carry their source document ID. The result is a
   heterogeneous graph with fact nodes, source nodes, and relation edges.
 2 Reasoning via Constrained Path Search. On the evidence graph, perform beam
   search over paths that start from the query, traverse at least one fact from
   each of (k \geq2) distinct sources, and terminate at a candidate answer.
   Paths are scored by a learned coherence function that rewards (a) internal
   logical consistency, (b) coverage of distinct sources, and (c) minimal
   reliance on contradiction edges. The top-3 paths are aggregated via a
   lightweight pointer network to produce the final answer.
 3 Answer Verification. A separate verifier module (a small T5-3B fine-tuned on
   synthetic multi-source entailment data) checks whether the aggregated answer
   is entailed by the union of facts on the selected path. If not, the system
   falls back to the highest-scoring path's answer.

Models are kept small (DeBERTa-v3-base, T5-3B) to avoid conflating scale with
method efficacy.

Dataset / BenchmarkMultiSourceQA — a constructed benchmark derived from HotpotQA
(multi-hop) and FEVER (claim verification) by sampling questions whose
ground-truth evidence spans3–5 Wikipedia documents. To test genuine multi-source
reasoning, we filter out questions solvable with any single document. Final
size:2,500 queries (1,500 train,500 dev,500 test), each with10 retrieved
passages (5 relevant,5 distracting). Source identity is preserved.

We also evaluate on the MuSiQue (Multi-Source Question) dataset as an
out-of-domain generalization test (2,000 questions, no explicit source
supervision).

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: Exact-match accuracy on the test set.

 • Secondary: F1 (token-level overlap), source-coverage rate (fraction of
   correct answers where the model used facts from ≥3 distinct sources),
   contradiction-handling accuracy (on a held-out subset of200 queries with
   known inter-source contradictions).
 • Robustness: Performance under increasing numbers of distracting passages
   (10,15,20 retrieved docs).

Baselines1. Flat RAG — standard retrieve-then-read with a single-pass T5-3B
reader (no explicit multi-source structure).

 2 Chain-of-Thought RAG — retrieved passages concatenated with a "think step by
   step" prompt, decoded with the same T5-3B.
 3 GraphRAG (no source tagging) — same evidence graph pipeline but source IDs
   are stripped from nodes (tests whether source identity matters beyond graph
   structure).
 4 Oracle retrieval — upper bound: only the gold evidence passages are provided
   (no distractors), same pipeline.

AblationsAll ablations are performed on the dev set,3 seeds each, with95%
confidence intervals:

 1 -fact-graph — replace the structured graph with a flat concatenation of
   extracted facts, scored by TF-IDF similarity (no relation edges, no path
   search). Isolates the contribution of graph structure.
 2 -source-tagging — node features exclude source ID. Tests whether provenance
   information drives the improvement.
 3 -relation-edge — the relation classifier is replaced with a uniform
   "unrelated" label for all cross-source pairs (no support/contradict edges).
   Tests the contribution of explicit relation modeling.
 4 -verifier — skip the final entailment verification step, directly output the
   aggregated path answer.
 5 +random-sources — shuffle the mapping between fact nodes and source
   documents. A sanity-check ablation: if source ID matters, this should degrade
   performance.

Expected Failure Modes1. Fact extraction noise. If the fact-triplet extractor
produces too many spurious or incomplete facts, the graph becomes dense with
low-precision edges. Expected signal: extraction precision <60% on the dev set →
the graph-based approach may not outperform flat RAG.

 2 Beam search collapse. With many unrelated facts, beam search may converge to
   locally coherent but globally wrong paths. Expected indicator: the top-3
   aggregation step selects the same answer as the top-1 path >90% of the time →
   the path diversity is insufficient.
 3 Distractor dominance. As the number of distracting passages increases
   beyond15, precision in the relation classifier drops, causing contradiction
   edges to be missed. The method may revert to bag-of-tokens behavior.
 4 OOD transfer gap. On MuSiQue, where source boundaries are implicit, the
   source-tagging component may not transfer. Expected degradation of8–12 points
   absolute vs. in-domain performance.

Limitations- The pipeline introduces multiple trainable components (fact
extraction, relation classification, path coherence scoring, verifier), each
requiring its own labeled data. End-to-end training is not feasible with current
data scales.

 • The beam search over the evidence graph has worst-case complexity (O(B \cdot
   |F|^2)) per query, where (|F|) is the number of fact nodes. For more than20
   retrieved passages, inference latency may exceed10 seconds per query on a
   single GPU.
 • MultiSourceQA is built from existing QA datasets and inherits their
   annotation biases (e.g., Wikipedia-centric, factoid-heavy). The method's
   effectiveness on open-domain, narrative, or multi-modal sources is untested.
 • The ablation is a single pass: without cross-run memory evolution, there is
   no mechanism to accumulate findings about which component fails at which data
   density, to transfer that insight to future experiments, or to adapt the
   pipeline architecture across runs. The proposal is frozen at its current
   design and cannot self-correct.

Research Proposal: Conflict-Aware Multi-Source Reasoning### Title
Conflict-Aware
Multi-Source Reasoning: Detecting and Resolving Information Conflicts in
Retrieval-Augmented Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat retrieved
documents as mutually consistent and complementary. This assumption breaks under
real-world conditions: sources contradict each other, report information at
different granularities, reflect different perspectives, or contain outright
errors. The result is that models either silently hallucinate a compromise,
arbitrarily follow one source while ignoring others, or produce incoherent
answers without signaling uncertainty. No existing benchmark or method
systematically addresses structured conflict adjudication as a first-class
reasoning step.

Key open question: Can explicit modeling of inter-source conflicts — their type,
severity, and resolvability — improve the factual accuracy and transparency of
multi-source reasoning?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Explicitly modeling inter-source conflicts through a structured
conflict graph + adjudication module will improve both factual accuracy and
answer coherence over standard RAG pipelines on multi-source QA tasks. The
improvement will be largest when retrieved passages are heterogeneous in content
or disagree on specific claims. The model will also benefit from learning when
to abstain rather than force an answer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
A four-stage pipeline:

1 Retrieval — Retrieve top-k passages for a query using a standard retriever
(e.g., Contriever-MS MARCO or ColBERT-v2).
2 Conflict Graph Construction — Build a fully connected graph where each node
is a retrieved passage. For each pair of passages, classify the edge as one
of: agreement, contradiction, complement (non-overlapping but
non-conflicting), or unrelated. Use an NLI-style classifier (e.g., fine-tuned
DeBERTa on paired passages) or an LLM-as-judge (e.g., GPT-4o-mini with
structured prompting). Edge weights encode confidence.
3 Conflict-Aware Aggregation — A lightweight adjudication module that takes the
conflict graph and the query, and produces:

• A set of reconciled facts (claims that survive cross-source verification)
• A set of irresolvable conflicts (contradictory claims the model cannot
adjudicate given available evidence)
• An optional abstain decision: if irresolvable conflicts touch the core of the
query, output "insufficient evidence" instead of forcing an answer.

4 Generation — An LM generates the final answer conditioned on the reconciled
facts and flagged conflicts, with an option to cite which passages support
each claim.

answer are directly supported by at least one retrieved passage (measured by
an NLI verifier)

Does allowing abstention hurt accuracy on answerable queries? | | Source

contexts).

Optimizing both jointly is non-trivial and requires a careful loss weighting
or Pareto-front analysis.

passage that does not support the specific claim it is attached to. A
secondary faithfulness check (e.g., fine-grained NLI per claim-passage pair)
may be needed as a guardrail.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Difficulty Filtering for Domain-Specific Language
Model Pretraining## Title
AdaFilter: Adaptive Difficulty-Aware Data Filtering for
Domain-Specific Language Model Pretraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Domain-specific language models (e.g., BioBERT, CodeBERT, FinBERT,
Legal-BERT) are typically pretrained from scratch or continually trained on a
curated corpus of in-domain text. A critical but understudied bottleneck is how
to filter which documents from the domain corpus are actually useful for
downstream performance. Current practice relies on heuristics (perplexity
thresholds, hand-crafted rules, or simple length/n-gram filters) that are noisy,
domain-agnostic, and oblivious to the model's current state during training. The
result is wasted compute on low-quality or redundant documents and, in some
cases, performance degradation from noisy data.

Concrete gap: No existing method jointly models (a) document quality, (b)
difficulty relative to the model's evolving capabilities, and (c) domain
relevance in a unified, trainable filtering pipeline. Prior work treats these
dimensions separately or uses static filtering that does not adapt during
training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A trainable, difficulty-aware filtering module that scores documents
along three axes — domain relevance, linguistic quality, and current-model
difficulty — and dynamically selects a curriculum of documents during
pretraining will produce a domain-specific LM with better perplexity and
downstream task performance than static heuristic filtering, while reducing
total training tokens by ≥20%.

Null hypothesis: Adaptive difficulty filtering yields no statistically
significant improvement in downstream performance over static heuristic
filtering (perplexity, F1, or accuracy) when matched for total compute.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
We propose AdaFilter, a three-stage filtering framework integrated into
the training loop.

Stage1: Relevance Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

Use a small, efficient classifier (e.g., a FastText or MiniLM-based model) to
score each document against a set of domain-defining seed keywords or exemplars.
This is a lightweight binary classifier trained on a small hand-labeled set (~1K
documents per domain). Documents below a relevance threshold are discarded
before training begins.

Stage2: Quality Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

For surviving documents, compute three quality signals:

• Perplexity under a small reference LM (e.g., a125M-parameter general-domain
model) — anomalously high PPL flags gibberish.
• Repetition ratio — fraction of repeated n-grams (n=8).
• Information density — ratio of unique tokens to total tokens. Combine into a
scalar quality score via a learned linear weighting (trained on a held-out
quality-labeled set).

Stage3: Adaptive Difficulty Curricula (online, per-epoch)

During training, maintain a difficulty estimator — a small MLP that takes the
model's current token-level embeddings for the first K tokens of a document and
predicts a difficulty score. Documents are bucketed into Easy/Medium/Hard bins.
The training sampler draws:

• **Epoch1-2:**80% Easy,15% Medium,5% Hard (warm-up)
• **Epoch3-5:**40% Easy,40% Medium,20% Hard- **Epoch6+:**10% Easy,40%
Medium,50% HardThe difficulty estimator is updated every N steps to track the
model's evolving state.

Training Protocol- Continual pretraining (MLM objective) starting from a
general-domain checkpoint (e.g., RoBERTa-base).

• Compare against: (a) unfiltered data, (b) static perplexity-filtered data,
(c) random subset of equal size, (d) random subset of equal compute.
• Each condition is run with3 random seeds for statistical reliability.
• Downstream evaluation every5K steps using a held-out set of domain tasks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We propose two domains for generalizability:

1 Biomedical: CORD-19 + PubMed abstracts (~2M documents). Downstream: BioASQ
(QA), ChemProt (RE), PubMedQA.
2 Legal: Pile-of-Law subset + EURLex (~1M documents). Downstream: CaseHOLD
(NLI), LexGLUE benchmark.

Each domain provides a clean test of whether domain-specific filtering matters
beyond generic heuristics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Category | Metric | Target |

|---|---|---| | Language modeling | Validation perplexity | Primary | |
Downstream tasks | Macro F1 / Accuracy (domain-specific benchmarks) | Primary |
| Efficiency | Training tokens to match baseline best performance | Secondary |
| Curriculum effect | Per-bin difficulty distribution over epochs | Analysis | |
Ablation | Delta from removing each AdaFilter component | Diagnostic |

All metrics reported with95% confidence intervals across3 seeds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|---|---| | No Filter | All domain documents, no curation | | PPL Threshold |
Documents with PPL < median under general-domain LM | | Heuristic | Length +
n-gram repetition filter (common practice) | | Random Subset (size-matched) |
Same number of documents as AdaFilter, randomly sampled | | Random Subset
(compute-matched) | Same number of training steps as AdaFilter, randomly sampled
| | DSIR | Importance resampling using n-gram hashing (Xie et al.,2023) | |
FastText Relevance Only | AdaFilter Stage1 alone |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No difficulty curriculum — Stage3 replaced with uniform sampling
from filtered pool → isolates curriculum contribution.

2 No quality scoring — Skip Stage2; only relevance + difficulty → isolates
quality signal.
3 Static buckets — Difficulty bins fixed at epoch1, never updated → isolates
benefit of adaptive difficulty.
4 Single domain — Run only on biomedical → tests domain transfer of findings.
5 Swap reference LM — Use a350M instead of125M reference model for perplexity →
tests sensitivity to reference size.
6 Score-to-weight variant — Instead of bucketing, weight documents by soft
difficulty score during loss → tests granularity benefit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Difficulty estimator collapses — becomes constant after a few epochs
| Add entropy regularization to bin assignment; monitor bin balance | |
Relevance classifier is the sole driver of gains (Stages2+3 add nothing) | If
ablation1 shows no degradation, the proposal still contributes an automated
relevance filter, which is a publishable result; reframe contribution around
end-to-end filtering | | Perplexity improves but downstream does not | Switch
primary evaluation to downstream tasks; analyze whether the LM is overfitting to
domain distribution at the expense of generalization | | High variance across
seeds | Increase to5 seeds; use paired bootstrap for significance testing | |
Adaptive curriculum underperforms static curriculum | Report honestly as
negative result with analysis of why — possibly because the domain corpus is too
homogeneous for curricula to matter | | Computational overhead of online
difficulty estimation outweighs token savings | Measure wall-clock time per1K
steps; if overhead >5%, treat as constraint and propose a cheaper proxy (e.g.,
loss on first128 tokens) | | Quality signals are highly correlated (redundant) |
Use PCA or mutual-information analysis on quality features; if redundancy is
high, the linear weighting in Stage2 will naturally down-weight correlated
features |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Success CriteriaThis proposal is considered successful if both conditions hold:

1 AdaFilter achieves statistically significant (p <0.05) improvement over all
baselines on at least one primary metric (perplexity or downstream F1) in
both domains.
2 AdaFilter uses ≤80% of the training tokens required by the best baseline to
reach the same downstream performance.

If only one domain shows gains, the contribution is domain-specific but still
publishable with the appropriate qualification.
