LongRoPE-Extended: Token-Level Positional Granularity for Extreme Long-Context
 LLMs## ProblemLarge Language Models (LLMs) continue to struggle with coherent
 reasoning over very long sequences (128K+ tokens). Existing position encoding
 extensions—RoPE, ALiBi, YaRN, NTK-aware scaling—either saturate in perplexity
    beyond a critical context length or exhibit a sharp "lost-in-the-middle"
     degradation where information placed at the center of long contexts is
 effectively invisible to the model. Current approaches treat position encoding
as a monolithic interpolation (frequency scaling), which fails because different
   attention heads and different token positions require distinct degrees of
    position sensitivity. The core problem is that positional expressiveness
  collapses as the sequence grows: distant positions become indistinguishable
under uniform frequency scaling, destroying the model's ability to retrieve and
                     compose information across long spans.

HypothesisDecomposing position encoding into head-adaptive frequency bands and
token-level position gating will preserve long-context perplexity and retrieval
accuracy beyond128K tokens. Specifically, each attention head selects a learned
mixture of low-frequency (coarse, long-range) and high-frequency (fine, local)
position components via a lightweight head-specific gating vector. Additionally,
each token learns to dynamically modulate its position sensitivity through a
context-dependent position-awareness gate conditioned on its own hidden state.
This dual mechanism jointly ensures that (a) heads specializing in long-range
dependency can maintain discriminative position signals even at extreme
distances, and (b) tokens in information-dense regions can sharpen their
position resolution while tokens in sparse regions can generalize across longer
gaps.

MethodLongRoPE-Extended modifies the rotary position encoding (RoPE) in an
existing long-context LLM (e.g., Llama-3-70B with YaRN scaling) with two
additive modules:

 1 Head-Adaptive Frequency Decomposition. Instead of applying a single frequency
   set to all attention heads, we maintain a bank of K base frequency groups
   (e.g., K=4), each with distinct rotary frequencies covering different ranges.
   Each head learns a soft assignment vector α_h ∈ R^K (via a lightweight MLP
   with a softmax output) that mixes these frequency groups at every forward
   pass. This allows head5, for instance, to attend strongly to nearby tokens
   (high-frequency mixture) while head20 attends to document-level dependencies
   (low-frequency mixture)—all within the same layer and without increasing the
   total parameter count beyond the small assignment MLP (≈0.01% of total
   params).
 2 Token-Level Position Gating. After RoPE is applied, each token computes a
   scalar position-awareness gate g_t = σ(W_g h_t + b_g) where h_t is the
   token's hidden state before the attention computation. The position encoding
   is then modulated: PE'_t = g_t · PE_t + (1 - g_t) · PĒ, where PĒ is a learned
   position-agnostic embedding. Intuitively, tokens that carry critical
   information (e.g., a cited number or a named entity) can "dial up" their
   position sensitivity to maintain fine-grained retrieval, while filler tokens
   (e.g., stopwords in the middle of a long passage) can relax positional
   constraints to reduce noise. This gate is applied independently per token per
   layer.

Training. We fine-tune Llama-3-70B on a mixture of three data sources: (a) the
Long-Synthetic dataset (randomly inserted key-value facts at varying depths),
(b) subsets of Proof-Pile-2 filtered for documents >64K tokens, and (c)
carefully selected slices of RedPajama-V2 with artificially inserted
cross-document dependency chains. We train for8K steps with a linear warmup and
cosine decay, using a learning rate of2e-5 and a batch size of128.

Inference. No overhead beyond the per-head soft assignment and per-token sigmoid
gate—both add <0.5% latency on a single A100-80GB at128K context.

Dataset / BenchmarkWe evaluate on the full suite of the RULER benchmark
(Needle-in-a-Haystack variants for retrieval, multi-needle, multi-query, and
variable-token-position tasks) and on LongBench (English subsets: QMSum, Qasper,
NarrativeQA, HotpotQA, MultiFieldQA-En, TREC, TriviaQA, SAMSum, and GovReport).
We additionally include the SCROLLS dataset (ContractNLI, SummScreen) and the
L-Eval suite for long-document QA. For stress-testing beyond128K, we construct a
synthetic "Mosaic Retrieval" task inspired by the work of Liu et al. (2024):
facts are inserted at20 equally spaced positions across a256K-token sequence,
and the model must retrieve all of them. This test exposes whether positional
resolution collapses at extreme lengths.

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: Passkey retrieval accuracy (single needle) at
depths0%,25%,50%,75%,100% across sequence lengths4K,8K,16K,32K,64K,128K, and256K
tokens. Reported as accuracy per depth bin.

 • Secondary: LongBench average F1 / Rouge-L score across all subsets.
 • Tertiary: Mosaic Retrieval F1 (mean retrieval accuracy over all20 needles
   per256K sequence).
 • Diagnostic: Per-head frequency diversity (entropy of α_h distributions across
   heads), position-gate statistics (mean and variance of g_t per token type,
   per position bin, and per layer). These diagnostics are used only for
   analysis, not as optimization targets.

Baselines| Method | Description |

|---|---| | Full-RoPE (no scaling) | Original Llama-3-70B without any extension
(max8K context, evaluated at all lengths regardless—fails beyond8K, establishes
the unextended floor). | | YaRN | Frequency interpolation with temperature
scaling. A direct frequency-engineering competitor. | | NTK-aware | Neural
Tangent Kernel-inspired frequency scaling. | | SelfExtend | Grouped attention
with two position scopes. | | LongRoPE | The non-evolutionary baseline that
inspired this work—learned frequency rescaling (no head-adaptive or token-level
components). |

All baselines are evaluated under identical fine-tuning conditions (same data,
same8K-step schedule, same LoRA rank-64 setup for comparability). Full
fine-tuning is used only for the proposed method; baselines use LoRA to keep
compute feasible.

Ablations1. w/o Head-Adaptive Frequencies. Remove the head-specific frequency
assignment; all heads share a single trained frequency bank. Tests whether
head-specific mixing is essential or just a result of overparameterization.

   position encoding. Tests whether token-level position modulation matters
   beyond the head-adaptive frequencies.
 3 Static Frequency Bank. Replace the learned α_h with a fixed hand-designed
   assignment (half heads low-frequency, half high-frequency). Tests whether the
   soft assignment is learning anything beyond a static partition.
 4 Single Training Stage. Remove the data-mixture curriculum (present all data
   from step0) to test whether the training schedule interacts with the position
   gating mechanism.
 5 Parameter Count Control. Reduce the base model's hidden dimension by0.01%
   (matching the added gate parameters) to verify that improvements are not
   simply from adding parameters.

Expected Failure Modes- Frequency collapse. The soft assignment MLP may converge
to a uniform mixture across heads, effectively reverting to the single-frequency
baseline. We mitigate this by initializing α_h with a Dirichlet prior that
favors sparse assignments and monitoring per-head entropy during training as a
diagnostic.

   may produce divergent behavior on sequences longer than any seen during
   training. We include256K-length synthetic data in the training mixture (≈5%
   of steps) to expose the model to extreme positions during fine-tuning.
 • Benchmark contamination. LongBench subsets may overlap with the RedPajama-V2
   training data. We explicitly filter against the LongBench evaluation sets
   using13-gram overlap deduplication (following the standard practice of Chen

Research Proposal: Structured Memory Banks for Long-Context Grounding in LLMs##
Title
Memory-Augmented Hierarchical Summarization (MAHS): Improving Long-Context
Grounding Without Full Attention Retraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models suffer from the lost-in-the-middle problem — when
prompted with documents exceeding ~8K tokens, accuracy on facts located in the
middle of the context degrades sharply, even for models that claim128K+ context
windows. Two root causes: (1) softmax attention dilutes signal across many
tokens, and (2) positional encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) lose relative resolution at
extreme lengths. Existing solutions (ring attention, sparse attention,
state-space models) either require expensive full retraining or sacrifice recall
on mid-context facts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Injecting a separately trained, retrieval-augmented memory bank —
built from hierarchically compressed chunks of the input context — into the
LLM's cross-attention layers will recover mid-context fact recall to within90%
of short-context performance without fine-tuning the base LLM. The memory bank
acts as a "second path" that bypasses diluted full-context attention.

Component1 — Hierarchical Chunking & Summarization

• Split the input context into fixed-size chunks (e.g.,512 tokens each).
• For each chunk, generate a short natural-language summary (<=64 tokens) using
a lightweight LM (e.g., Phi-3-mini). This forms the first summary layer.
• Recursively apply the same process to the summary sequence to produce a
second, coarser summary layer.
• Store all chunks and summaries in a flat key-value store keyed by chunk
position and semantic embedding.

Component2 — Retrieval-Augmented Memory Attention

• Insert a small set of memory tokens (e.g.,128) at the start of each attention
layer's key-value cache during generation.
• At each decoding step, retrieve the top-k chunks/summaries (by cosine
similarity to the current hidden state) from the memory bank.
• Encode the retrieved chunks as additional key-value pairs appended to the
existing full-context KV cache for that layer, but with a separate learned
gating scalar that down-weights the full-context path when memory retrieval
has high confidence.

Component3 — Training (Lightweight)

• Freeze the base LLM entirely.
• Train only the memory encoder (a small transformer, ~50M params), the
retrieval projection layer, and the gating scalars.
• Training objective: next-token prediction on long-document perplexity, with
an auxiliary contrastive loss that pulls the hidden state closer to the
embedding of the chunk containing the ground-truth next token.

Title: ValueCartography: A Systematic Framework for Measuring and Steering
Cross-Cultural Value Alignment in Large Language Models---

ProblemCurrent LLM alignment research operates under a tacit assumption of
universality — RLHF, constitutional AI, and preference-tuning pipelines
overwhelmingly use English-language, WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized,
Rich, Democratic) annotator pools. This produces models that appear "aligned" on
standard benchmarks (HH-RLHF, Anthropic's helpfulness/harmlessness) but encode a
narrow cultural value profile. When deployed globally, these models exhibit
measurable shifts in judgment across moral dilemmas, social norms, and even
factual framing (e.g., individualism vs. collectivism in advice-giving). The
core problem is twofold: (1) no systematic methodology exists to map an LLM's
value distribution onto established cross-cultural value dimensions (Hofstede,
Schwartz, World Values Survey), and (2) no training-time intervention has been
shown to steer that distribution along culturally meaningful axes without
degrading general capabilities.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisA taxonomically grounded, multi-scale evaluation framework — anchored
in validated cross-cultural psychology instruments — can reliably measure LLM
value enculturation across at least six cultural axes. Furthermore, using
culturally stratified preference data constructed from paired judgments across
these axes, direct preference optimization (DPO) can shift model outputs along a
specified cultural dimension by at least0.5σ on that axis while maintaining <2%
degradation on MMLU and BBH. The null hypothesis is that LLM value profiles are
dominated by pretraining corpus distribution (English internet) and resist
targeted steering beyond superficial token-level shifts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MethodThe approach proceeds in three stages, each designed to isolate a specific
mechanism of cultural value encoding.

Stage1 — Cultural Value Probe Battery (CV-Probe). Build a multi-choice benchmark
structured around six cultural dimensions drawn from Hofstede
(individualism–collectivism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance, long-term
orientation, indulgence–restraint) and the Schwartz Value Survey (openness to
change vs. conservation, self-enhancement vs. self-transcendence). For each
dimension, generate50–80 minimal-pair scenarios where two completions express
opposing cultural poles. Scenarios are sourced from existing cross-cultural
psychology vignettes (WVS items, GLOBE project scenarios) adapted to an
LLM-inference format. Each item is validated by at least three human raters per
target culture (US, China, India, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, Germany — six cultures
spanning the major value clusters). Models output a forced choice plus a
confidence rating. The probe returns a6-dimensional value vector with confidence
intervals.

Stage2 — Culturally Stratified Preference Dataset (CulPaD). Sample10,000 prompts
from open-ended generation corpora (ShareGPT, Alpaca, Dolly). For each prompt,
generate two candidate responses from a base model (Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B).
Annotators from each target culture rank responses on both helpfulness and
cultural appropriateness. The dataset is stratified so that each of the6
cultures contributes ~1,600 preference pairs, allowing within-culture and
cross-culture analyses. This enables both fine-tuning toward a specific cultural
profile and training of a culture-conditional reward model.

Stage3 — Steering via Culturally-Conditioned DPO (CC-DPO). Train a base model
(Llama-3-8B) using DPO on CulPaD under three conditions: (1) monocultural —
preference data from a single culture (US only); (2) multicultural — pooled
preferences across all cultures, randomly sampled; (3) culturally-conditioned —
preferences are paired with a culture token prepended to the prompt (e.g.,
[CULTURE: India] ...). The culturally-conditioned variant tests whether the
model can learn to modulate its value profile based on cultural context at
inference time, rather than converging to a single averaged profile. Each
condition uses identical hyperparameters (β=0.1, learning rate2e-6,3 epochs),
varying only the data distribution.

vignettes + expert-curated minimal pairs |400 items (6 dimensions × ~67 items) |
| CulPaD | Responses from base model + human rankings (6 cultures) |10,000
preference pairs | | Evaluation | CV-Probe scores + MMLU + BBH + TruthfulQA +
culture-specific holdout | Standard splits |

For cross-validation, each culture's preference pairs in CulPaD are held out

Title: CULTURAL-PREF: Preference Tuning with Culturally-Grounded Contrastive
Examples for Cross-Cultural LLM AlignmentProblem. Current RLHF/DPO alignment
pipelines overwhelmingly use preference data annotated by English-speaking,
Western raters. This produces models that (a) treat Western cultural norms as
universal defaults, (b) give culturally inappropriate or offensive answers in
non-Western contexts, and (c) lack measurable mechanisms to control which
cultural frame the model should adopt for a given user or query. No existing
work has systematically decomposed which dimensions of alignment (helpfulness,
harmlessness, honesty, social norms) are most culturally divergent, nor tested
whether targeted preference data can close the gap without degrading Western
performance.

Hypothesis. Fine-tuning an LLM with preference pairs where the same query
receives different culturally appropriate responses across target cultures
(e.g., Japanese vs. Brazilian vs. Saudi Arabian social norms) will produce a
model whose outputs can be steered toward a specified cultural frame via a
lightweight prompt prefix, while maintaining competitive performance on standard
Western-centric benchmarks. The core claim: cultural divergence in alignment is
concentrated in a small set of behavioral dimensions (social hierarchy,
indirectness, taboo topics, gift-giving norms, and individualist vs.
collectivist framing), and targeted contrastive examples on these dimensions
suffice to induce generalizable cross-cultural behavior.

Method. Three-stage pipeline:

1 Taxonomy construction. Use a research-agent-assisted literature review of
cross-cultural psychology (Hofstede dimensions, GLOBE project, Hall's
high/low context) and existing culturally-aware LLM datasets (CULTURALBENCH,
CULTUREPAIR, GLOBALALIGN) to produce a taxonomy of8–12 behavioral dimensions
where LLM outputs are expected to diverge across cultures. Each dimension
gets a one-paragraph annotation specifying the expected range of appropriate
behavior.
2 Contrastive preference dataset. For each dimension, generate200–400
query-response triples (query, culturally-appropriate-response-A,
culturally-appropriate-response-B) across two target cultures (e.g.,
US-English and Japanese) using human annotation or validated LLM-as-judge
pipelines with culture-specific rubrics. Each triple explicitly labels which
cultural frame each response fits. Total target: ~3,000–5,000 preference
pairs.
3 Preference tuning & steering. Fine-tune a base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B or
Qwen-2.5-7B) via DPO on the contrastive dataset. Add a steering mechanism: a
prepended system prompt specifying the target cultural frame (e.g., "You are
a helpful assistant responding to someone in Japan. Follow Japanese social
norms: use polite register, avoid direct refusals, respect hierarchical
address."). Evaluate whether steering via prompt alone suffices or whether a
lightweight adapter (LoRA per culture) is needed.

Dataset / Benchmark.

• Training: Custom constructed dataset (described above).
• Evaluation: CULTURALBENCH (cross-cultural QA and social norms), CULTUREPAIR
(culturally sensitive comparison pairs), and a subset of GLOBALALIGN (moral
and social alignment across10+ countries). Also construct a held-out
"cross-cultural adversarial" test set of200 prompts where the appropriate
response differs sharply between two cultures (e.g., feedback to a superior,
gift refusal, discussion of religious holidays).

Evaluation Metrics.

• Cultural appropriateness score: Agreement with human raters from each target
culture (≥3 raters per item, Krippendorff's α ≥0.7 threshold) on a5-point
Likert scale measuring whether the response is culturally appropriate for the
specified frame.
• Steerability accuracy: For each culture-steered query, does the model's
response align with the intended culture (vs. default/majority culture)?
Measured by both human evaluation and an LLM judge fine-tuned on the same
taxonomy.
• Western benchmark retention: Performance drop on HellaSwag, MMLU, and
MT-Bench. Threshold: ≤2% absolute degradation.
• Dimension-level divergence: Per-dimension score showing which cultural
dimensions the model handles well vs. poorly.

Baselines.

1 Base model (no fine-tuning): Shows the default cultural bias of the
pretrained model.
2 Standard DPO (general preference data): Trained on the full HelpSteer2 or
UltraFeedback dataset (no cultural conditioning). Measures whether standard
alignment already produces monocultural outputs.
3 Naive prompt steering: Apply the same culture-steering prompt to the base
model without fine-tuning. Isolates the effect of prompting vs. preference
tuning.
4 Culture-agnostic DPO + prompt steering: DPO on the contrastive dataset
without culture labels during training, but with steering prompts at
inference. Tests whether contrastive data alone helps even without labeled
training.

Ablations.

• Dimension ablation: Remove one behavioral dimension at a time from the
contrastive dataset. Which dimensions are critical for cross-cultural
generalization?
• Data scaling: Train on10%,25%,50%,100% of the contrastive dataset. Is there a
diminishing-returns threshold?
• Model scale: Repeat the best configuration on a1B,7B, and27B parameter model
(or whatever sizes are available). Does cross-cultural steerability scale
with model size?
• Target culture ablation: Train on US–Japan pairs only, then evaluate on
US–Brazil and US–Saudi Arabia. Does the method generalize to unseen target
cultures?

Expected Failure Modes.

1 Surface-level mimicry. The model learns to insert polite markers and
culture-specific keywords without understanding deeper social norms (e.g.,
produces Japanese honorifics but gives a direct refusal that violates
Japanese indirectness norms). Mitigation: Include examples where the surface
form and deep norm diverge, and evaluate with adversarial probes that test
for this distinction.
2 Steering interference. The culture-steering prompt competes with the base
model's pre-existing alignment (refusal training, safety filters), producing
unpredictable behavior in safety-critical queries. Mitigation: Explicitly
include edge-case safety prompts in the contrastive dataset and measure
safety metric separately.
3 Overfitting to stereotype. The taxonomy-based approach encodes stereotypical
or outdated cultural norms, producing responses that caricature rather than
respect the target culture. Mitigation: Validate all dimension annotations
with in-culture reviewers; include intra-cultural variation examples (e.g.,
both formal and informal Japanese responses).
4 Western performance collapse. Teaching the model to deviate from its default
alignment causes broad degradation on standard English benchmarks.
Mitigation: Monitor Western benchmarks throughout training, early-stop if
degradation exceeds2%, and test whether a residual connection or adapter
merging strategy preserves base capabilities.
5 Rater disagreement. Human raters from the same culture disagree on what
constitutes an appropriate response, making the ground-truth labels noisy.
Mitigation: Use an agreement threshold (Krippendorff's α ≥0.7) and discard or
re-annotate items below it. Report confidence intervals on all human
evaluation metrics.
6 Non-transferability to unseen cultures. The model learns a mapping from
"culture token → behavior" but fails on cultures not seen during training.
Mitigation: The target-culture ablation (train on US–Japan, test on
US–Brazil, US–Saudi Arabia) directly tests this; if it fails, the method
collapses to a retrieval problem rather than actual cultural generalization.

Research Proposal: Stabilizing Value Alignment for Multi-Agent Systems via
 Reciprocal Reward Shaping## TitleConvergent Value Alignment: Reciprocal Reward
          Shaping for Norm Emergence in Heterogeneous Agent Societies

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ProblemValue alignment — ensuring AI agents act in accordance with human values
— becomes radically more difficult in multi-agent settings. When independently
aligned agents interact, emergent behaviors often violate the very values each
agent was trained to uphold: competing reward functions produce reward hacking,
value drift, and Pareto-suboptimal equilibria (e.g., speculative cooperation
collapses under distribution shift). Existing approaches treat alignment as a
per-agent property enforced at training time, then freeze it at deployment. This
static approach fails because:

 1 Value disambiguation is underspecified — a single principle (e.g., "do no
   harm") maps to different actions across contexts.
 2 Multi-agent dynamics create second-order effects — aligned agents can
   mutually destabilize each other's value functions.
 3 Norm emergence is unguided — societies of agents converge to conventions, but
   nothing guarantees those conventions are aligned with human values unless the
   reward structure explicitly shapes them.

The core problem: How can a population of heterogeneous agents converge to a
shared, stable set of aligned behaviors without centralized reward supervision
at runtime?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisReciprocal reward shaping — where each agent's reward function
includes a small learned term predicting the value-satisfaction of nearby agents
— causes a heterogeneous multi-agent system to converge to a Pareto-optimal
aligned equilibrium more reliably than either (a) individually aligned agents
with static reward functions or (b) agents shaped by a global reward signal.

Research Proposal: Steering Vector–Based Value Control in Large Language
Models## Title

Controllable AI Alignment

Problem
Current value alignment methods for LLMs — primarily RLHF and
constitutional AI — operate at the parametric level: they fine-tune model
weights using reward-model scores or self-critique data. This creates two
unresolved problems:

1 Value brittleness under distribution shift — an RLHF-tuned model may behave
consistently on in-distribution helpfulness/harmlessness prompts but fail on
adversarial inputs, domain shifts, or tasks that were not represented in the
preference data.
2 Value entanglement with capability — fine-tuning for alignment inevitably
modifies weights that also encode reasoning, factual recall, and linguistic
ability, making it difficult to attribute behavior changes to "value
learning" versus capability degradation or surface-level pattern matching.

A method that can separately control value-relevant behavior without modifying
base weights would enable testable hypotheses about whether alignment is a
representational property or a learned behavioral policy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary hypothesis: For a given LLM, there exists a low-dimensional
subspace in the residual stream (or attention head outputs) such that
intervention along a value direction — defined by contrasting activation
patterns on value-consistent vs. value-violating examples — shifts the model's
alignment-relevant generation behavior on held-out prompts with statistical
significance (p <0.01, Bonferroni-corrected across5 dimensions) while preserving
perplexity on standard language modeling benchmarks within2% of the unmodified
model.

dimensions (e.g., a "honesty" vector improves "fairness" behavior) but are

Self-supervised audio foundation models promise a single pretrained
backbone that transfers to speech, music, and environmental sound tasks. The
AudioMAE (Xu et al.,2022) architecture—an asymmetric encoder-decoder with a high
mask ratio (75–80%) applied to mel-spectrogram patches—claimed state-of-the-art
transfer on AudioSet, ESC-50, and Speech Commands v2. However, the community
lacks:

1 Independent reproduction — the original code was released late and the
results have not been systematically verified by a separate group.
2 A controlled comparison against reconstruction-based (AudioMAE) vs.
contrastive (CLAP, ImageBind) pretraining objectives for general-purpose use.
3 An ablation isolating what drives performance: high mask ratio, decoder
depth, or patch size?

We aim to reproduce AudioMAE's core results and extend them by introducing a
hybrid objective that combines masked reconstruction with a contrastive
alignment loss (audio-text), testing the hypothesis that reconstruction alone is
insufficient for general-purpose transfer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Null hypothesis (H₀): AudioMAE's masked reconstruction objective
yields representations that transfer to speech, music, and environmental tasks
as well as or better than a hybrid reconstruction + contrastive objective.

Alternative hypothesis (H₁): Adding a contrastive alignment loss (audio-text)
during pretraining significantly improves downstream transfer on tasks requiring
high-level semantics (e.g., audio captioning, zero-shot sound classification),
while maintaining or improving performance on acoustic-only tasks (e.g., scene
classification).

Falsification condition: If the hybrid model does not outperform AudioMAE on at
least2 out of3 semantic-level downstream tasks (by >2% absolute in the primary
metric) while not regressing by more than1% on acoustic-level tasks, H₁ is
rejected.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Stage1 — Reproduce AudioMAEExact reproduction of the AudioMAE baseline
(Xu et al.,2022) using the official configuration:

• Input: Log-mel spectrograms (128 mel bins,1024 FFT,512 hop), patchified
into16×16 patches (time×freq).
• Encoder: ViT-B/16 (12 layers,768 hidden,12 heads).
• Decoder: Lightweight4-layer ViT (384 hidden,6 heads).
• Mask ratio:80% of patches masked.
• Pretraining objective: L2 reconstruction loss in the spectrogram space
(normalized patches).
• Pretraining data: AudioSet-2M (balanced subset of ~2M clips from AudioSet).
• Optimization: AdamW, lr=1.5e-4, cosine decay, batch size1024,800 epochs.

pretraining,50% of batches use reconstruction loss and50% use the InfoNCE loss
aligning audio embeddings with paired text descriptions (from AudioSet labels +
synthetic captions via LaCLAP pipeline). Total loss: L = λ·L_recon +
(1-λ)·L_contrastive, with λ annealed from1.0 →0.5 across training.

separately, full fine-tuning) on each benchmark.
